study.summary: The basic verb 'to be': it states that something exists or is present ('there is'), links a subject to what it is ('X is Y'), and in Jesus' absolute 'I am' sayings it carries overtones of the divine name.

senses.label: Exist, have being
senses.definition: To be in existence, to have real being, as opposed to not existing or merely coming to be.
senses.note: Revelation's title ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ('who is and who was and who is to come'); τὰ μὴ ὄντα 'things that do not exist' (ROM 4:17).

senses.label: There is; have (with dative)
senses.definition: Impersonal 'there is / there was', asserting that something is to be found; with a dative of the person it expresses possession ('there was to them' = they had).
senses.note: ἔστιν + infinitive can mean 'it is possible' (HEB 9:5; 1CO 11:20).

senses.label: Be present, be somewhere
senses.definition: To be located in a place or with someone; of times and events, to be at hand or take place.
senses.note: Often with prepositions: εἶναι μετά (be with), ἐν, ἐκ (be from, originate in, JOH 3:31).

senses.label: Copula: is (identity, description)
senses.definition: Links a subject to a predicate noun or adjective, stating identity, class or quality.
senses.note: Often left unexpressed in Greek (nominal sentences); with a participle it forms periphrastic tenses (MAR 1:22; LUK 1:10; COL 1:6).

senses.label: Is = means, represents
senses.definition: In explanations of parables, figures and types, 'is' states what something signifies or stands for.
senses.note: τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν / ὅ ἐστιν 'that is', 'which means' introduces a gloss or translation (MAR 7:2; MAR 3:17).

senses.label: Belong to (with genitive)
senses.definition: With a genitive, to belong to someone or something, to be of his party, kind or possession.
senses.note: 'I am of Paul' (1CO 1:12) = I belong to Paul's faction; 'theirs is the kingdom' (MAT 5:3).

senses.label: Absolute 'I am' (ἐγώ εἰμι)
senses.definition: Used without an expressed predicate: 'It is I', 'I am he', or, in its weightiest uses, an absolute 'I am' echoing God's self-designation in the Greek Old Testament.
senses.note: Compare LXX ἐγώ εἰμι for Hebrew אֲנִי הוּא (DEU 32:39; ISA 43:10).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John builds Jesus' self-revelation on ἐγώ εἰμι, both with predicates (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and absolutely; Revelation names God 'who is and who was and who is to come'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke favours periphrastic imperfects (ἦν + present participle) for ongoing scenes, a style reminiscent of Semitic narrative.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses εἶναι with the genitive for belonging and allegiance: being 'of Christ' or of a party leader.

study.translationNote: The absolute ἐγώ εἰμι is rendered 'It is I' (MAR 6:50; JOH 6:20), 'I am he' (JOH 18:5) or simply 'I am' (JOH 8:58). The Greek is the same; translators choose according to how far they think the context recalls God's self-naming. Likewise 'is' in figurative statements (MAT 26:26; 1CO 10:4) is kept as 'is' in most versions, leaving readers to decide how literally to take it.

background.note: The Greek Old Testament renders God's 'I am he' (אֲנִי הוּא) with ἐγώ εἰμι, the background usually invoked for Jesus' absolute sayings.
The middle imperfect ἤμην, which replaces classical ἦ throughout the NT, is already well established in everyday Ptolemaic papyri.
Popular writing often substitutes ἦν for the subjunctive ᾖ after ἐάν, as in the letter of Hilarion; the same phenomenon appears in NT manuscripts.

study.exegesisTip: Note word order and the article in predicate statements (e.g. θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, JOH 1:1), and remember that Greek often omits 'is' altogether, so an English 'is' may not be in the text.
study.caution: Whether every ἐγώ εἰμι in the Gospels (e.g. MAR 6:50; JOH 6:20) deliberately echoes the divine name, or some are simple self-identification ('It's me'), is debated; so is how 'is' should be understood in the words of institution (MAT 26:26).

study.summary: The ordinary verb of speaking: to say, tell, assert or command; also to mean, to call or name. It focuses on the content of what is said rather than the act of uttering sounds.

senses.label: Say, speak
senses.definition: To express something in words, introducing direct speech, reported speech, or the content of a reply or question.
senses.note: Participle λέγων often just marks a quotation (like Hebrew לֵאמֹר); ἀπεκρίθη λέγων 'answered, saying'. Also of thought, λέγειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ 'say to oneself' (MAT 3:9) and of writing (PHP 4:11).

senses.label: Claim, assert, maintain
senses.definition: To affirm something as true, often with the implication that the claim is open to question.
senses.note: 'Whoever says he abides in him' (1JO 2:6) = whoever claims.

senses.label: Tell, command
senses.definition: To direct someone to do something; an authoritative instruction rather than mere information.
senses.note: Usually with infinitive or ἵνα; 'I say to you, do not swear' (MAT 5:34).

senses.label: Mean, refer to
senses.definition: To have someone or something in mind when speaking; to explain what one intends.
senses.note: Paul's λέγω δέ 'what I mean is' introduces clarification (1CO 1:12; GAL 4:1).

senses.label: Call, name
senses.definition: To designate someone by a name or title; passive 'be called, be named'.
senses.note: ὁ λεγόμενος 'who is called' frequently introduces names and titles (MAT 1:16).

senses.label: Scripture or God says
senses.definition: Used of Scripture, God or the prophets speaking, often in present tense to present the word as still addressing the hearer.
senses.note: τάδε λέγει 'thus says' (REV 2-3) echoes prophetic and royal-edict formulae.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: The antitheses of the Sermon on the Mount turn on ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, 'but I say to you', setting Jesus' authority alongside the received tradition.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John alone has the doubled ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν/σοι introducing solemn pronouncements.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark frequently uses the historic present λέγει ('he says') in narrative, giving vividness.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses λέγω to clarify or qualify his own argument, even distinguishing his word from the Lord's.

study.translationNote: Jesus' reply σὺ λέγεις / σὺ εἶπας (MAT 27:11; MAR 15:2) is rendered 'You have said so' (ESV) or 'Yes, it is as you say' (NIV). The Greek is a reserved formula: it accepts the words but throws responsibility back on the speaker, so versions differ on how affirmative to make it. Pleonastic 'saying' (λέγων) is also often dropped in modern versions.

background.note: λέγει / τάδε λέγει was the formal opening of edicts of emperors and magistrates, a background for the 'thus says' of the letters to the seven churches.
The sense 'tell, command' is found in everyday letters, e.g. money someone 'told you to give me'.
The LXX uses λέγει for the prophetic נְאֻם, 'declares (the LORD)'.

study.exegesisTip: Check whether λέγω introduces mere report, a claim, a command or a clarification ('I mean'); the English 'say' can hide each of these.
study.caution: The traditional distinction that λέγω stresses content while λαλέω stresses utterance is a broad tendency and should not be pressed in individual verses. Strong's numbering also splits forms of the one verb (εἶπον G2036, ἐρῶ G2046) from λέγω.

study.summary: God: in the NT almost always the one true God of Israel; it can also mean a pagan deity, and in a few key texts it is predicated of Jesus Christ.

senses.label: The one true God
senses.definition: The God of Israel, creator and sovereign, worshipped by Jews and Christians.
senses.note: Usually with the article, but anarthrous θεός regularly means the same God, esp. after prepositions and in genitive phrases (ROM 1:17; JOH 1:6).

senses.label: God as Father of Jesus
senses.definition: God identified specifically as the Father, especially in relation to Jesus and to believers.
senses.note: 'The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ'; in Paul 'God' usually denotes the Father, 'Lord' Jesus.

senses.label: Predicated of Christ
senses.definition: In a few passages θεός is applied to Jesus, affirming his divine identity.
senses.note: Several of these involve debated grammar, punctuation or textual variants (see caution).

senses.label: A god, pagan deity
senses.definition: Any being regarded as divine in polytheistic belief, or a person hailed as a god.
senses.note: Paul: 'so-called gods' that are 'by nature not gods' (1CO 8:5; GAL 4:8).

senses.label: Transferred: whatever rules a life
senses.definition: Applied to humans or things that hold divine-like authority or devotion over people.
senses.note: Judges as 'gods' (Ps 82:6 cited in JOH 10:34); 'their god is the belly' (PHP 3:19); Satan 'the god of this age' (2CO 4:4).

senses.label: Intensive: 'to God' = exceedingly
senses.definition: The dative τῷ θεῷ can function as a Hebraic superlative, 'very, in God's eyes'.
senses.note: Moses was ἀστεῖος τῷ θεῷ, 'exceedingly fair' or 'fair in God's sight' (ACT 7:20).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel opens and climaxes with θεός applied to the Word/Jesus, framing the whole book.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul pairs 'God the Father' with 'the Lord Jesus Christ' in greetings and confessions, adapting the Shema.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew normally says 'kingdom of heaven'; 'kingdom of God' appears only in a few places.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews applies Psalm 45's address 'O God' to the Son.

study.translationNote: JOH 1:1c (θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος) is rendered 'the Word was God' by nearly all versions; 'the Word was divine' (Moffatt, Goodspeed) or 'a god' (New World Translation) reflect different readings of the predicate noun without the article. Most grammarians hold that the article is omitted to mark θεός as predicate and to stress the Word's nature, not to make it indefinite. In TIT 2:13 and 2PE 1:1, 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (most modern versions) versus 'the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ' (KJV) turns on whether one article governs both nouns.

background.note: From Homer on θεός can denote the divine in general, 'God will grant this and withhold that'.
Rulers were hailed as gods: Ptolemy V on the Rosetta stone is 'god from god and goddess'.
An official is addressed 'to the god and lord', the same pairing as Thomas' confession in JOH 20:28.
The LXX calls judges 'gods' in the psalm Jesus quotes in John 10.

study.exegesisTip: Do not assume that θεός without the article means 'a god': after prepositions, in genitive phrases and as predicate it normally still refers to the one God or stresses what God is.
study.caution: Whether θεός refers to Christ is debated in several texts: the punctuation of ROM 9:5, the one-article construction in TIT 2:13, and the reading μονογενὴς θεός versus μονογενὴς υἱός in JOH 1:18. Whether JOH 1:1c is 'qualitative' or 'definite' is also discussed among grammarians.

study.summary: All, every, whole: πᾶς expresses totality, either distributively (every single one), collectively (the whole), or as 'every kind of'; neuter forms mean 'everything' or the universe.

senses.label: Every, each
senses.definition: With a noun without the article in the singular: every individual member of a class.
senses.note: With a negative, πᾶς ... οὐ = 'no one, nothing' (ROM 3:20; GAL 2:16).

senses.label: Every kind of, all sorts
senses.definition: All varieties of something, without implying every single instance.

senses.label: Full, utmost (with abstract nouns)
senses.definition: With nouns of quality or power: complete, the highest degree of.
senses.note: 'All authority' (MAT 28:18); 'all joy' = pure joy (JAM 1:2).

senses.label: Whole, entire
senses.definition: With the article (or a collective noun): the whole of a group or thing taken together.
senses.note: 'All Israel' (ROM 11:26) refers to the people as a whole.

senses.label: All people, everyone
senses.definition: Masculine forms used as a noun: everyone, all people; πᾶς ὁ + participle 'everyone who'.
senses.note: οἱ πάντες 'all (as a definite whole)' (ROM 11:32; EPH 4:13).

senses.label: All things, everything
senses.definition: Neuter: everything in a given context, or with the article τὰ πάντα the universe as a totality.
senses.note: Anarthrous πάντα = all things severally; τὰ πάντα = the whole created order.

senses.label: Adverbial phrases: always, in every way
senses.definition: In set prepositional phrases: διὰ παντός 'always', ἐν παντί 'in every way', πρὸ πάντων 'above all', κατὰ πάντα 'in every respect'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses τὰ πάντα for the whole cosmos created through and reconciled in Christ, and πάντες in sweeping statements about sin and salvation.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the neuter πᾶν (ὅ) collectively of persons, 'all that the Father gives me', stressing the group as a whole.

study.translationNote: Because πᾶς can mean 'every' or 'every kind of', versions differ: 1TI 6:10 is 'the root of all evil' (KJV) but 'a root of all kinds of evil' (NIV, ESV). In 1TI 2:4 most render 'all people', while some interpreters argue for 'all kinds of people'; the Greek allows debate, and context must decide.

background.note: In the LXX πᾶς chiefly renders Hebrew כֹּל, producing Hebraic expressions such as 'all flesh' for all humanity.

study.exegesisTip: Check number and article: anarthrous singular = 'every', with the article = 'the whole', neuter plural with the article = 'the universe'; then ask whether context limits the 'all'.
study.caution: The scope of 'all' in salvation texts (ROM 5:18; 1CO 15:22; COL 1:20; 1TI 2:4) is debated: all without exception, all without distinction, or all within a defined group (e.g. all who are in Christ).

study.summary: Lord, master: one with authority or ownership. It ranges from a polite 'sir' to the LXX's rendering of God's name, and becomes the central confession of Jesus' divine lordship.

senses.label: Owner, master, one in authority
senses.definition: A person who owns property or slaves, or has authority over others (master, owner, ruler, husband).
senses.note: With genitive of the thing ruled: 'lord of the vineyard', 'lord of the Sabbath' (MAT 12:8).

senses.label: Sir (polite address)
senses.definition: Vocative κύριε as a courteous form of address to a superior or stranger.
senses.note: When people address Jesus as κύριε in the Gospels, context must decide between respect and worship (MAT 8:2; MAT 8:25).

senses.label: God (the LORD)
senses.definition: The divine title standing for the God of Israel, especially where the LXX used it for the Hebrew divine name.
senses.note: Often anarthrous like a proper name in OT quotations ('angel of the Lord', 'Lord of Sabaoth').

senses.label: Jesus as exalted Lord
senses.definition: The title confessed of the risen Jesus, expressing his sovereign authority and sharing in God's own name.
senses.note: OT texts about the LORD are applied to Jesus (ROM 10:13; MAR 1:3).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke alone among the Synoptics regularly calls Jesus ὁ κύριος in narration during his ministry, and Acts proclaims him 'Lord and Christ'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's basic confession is 'Jesus is Lord'; he applies YHWH texts to him and describes Christian life as 'in the Lord'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John reserves the climactic confession for Thomas, 'My Lord and my God', and uses ὁ κύριος for the risen Jesus.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark rarely uses κύριος of Jesus; the Syrophoenician woman is the only person who addresses him as κύριε.

study.translationNote: English versions must decide in each vocative whether κύριε means 'Sir' or 'Lord' (e.g. JOH 4:11, 'Sir' in most modern versions), and in OT quotations whether to signal the divine name ('LORD' in small capitals is used in the OT but rarely in the NT). The single Greek word covers both levels.

background.note: The LXX uses κύριος chiefly for the divine name YHWH, which is why NT application of the title to Jesus carries divine weight.
κύριε is the normal respectful address to officials in petitions, 'my lord'.
Invitations to dine 'at the table of the lord Sarapis' parallel Paul's 'table of the Lord' (1CO 10:21).
Also used affectionately in family letters, e.g. a son to 'my father and lord'.

study.exegesisTip: In OT quotations check the Hebrew behind κύριος: where it stands for the divine name and is applied to Jesus (ROM 10:13; PHP 2:10-11), the author is making a high christological claim.
study.caution: How much the vocative κύριε implies in Gospel encounters is uncertain. Whether the earliest LXX manuscripts wrote κύριος or retained the Hebrew divine name is also debated, though NT authors clearly read κύριος.

study.summary: To come to be: to be born or arise, to happen, to be done, or to become something new. It describes change and coming-into-being, in contrast to εἰμί, which describes simple being.

senses.label: Come into being, be born, arise
senses.definition: To begin to exist, be born or created; of persons and phenomena, to appear or arise.
senses.note: Of times: 'when evening came' (MAT 14:15); of a public appearance (MAR 1:4; JOH 1:6).

senses.label: Happen, take place
senses.definition: Of events: to come to pass, occur; with dative, to befall someone.
senses.note: καὶ ἐγένετο 'and it came to pass' introduces narrative episodes (LXX וַיְהִי).

senses.label: Be done, be performed
senses.definition: To be carried out, accomplished or brought about, as of a will, a miracle or an ordinance.
senses.note: γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου 'your will be done' (MAT 6:10).

senses.label: Become
senses.definition: To pass into a new state or role, with a predicate noun or adjective.
senses.note: Aorist ἐγενήθη is equivalent to ἐγένετο in Koine and has no passive force.

senses.label: Be, come to be (in a place or state)
senses.definition: With prepositions or a dative: to arrive, find oneself in a condition, or belong to someone.
senses.note: 'I was in the Spirit' (REV 1:10); γενέσθαι ἀνδρί 'belong to (marry) a man' (ROM 7:3).

senses.label: μὴ γένοιτο: 'By no means!'
senses.definition: The optative wish 'may it not be' as an emphatic rejection of a wrong inference.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke imitates biblical narrative style with καὶ ἐγένετο / ἐγένετο δέ followed by a finite verb or infinitive.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's μὴ γένοιτο rejects a false conclusion drawn from his own argument, almost always after a rhetorical question.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John sets γίνομαι (coming into being) against εἰμί (eternal being): the Word 'was', all things 'came to be', the Word 'became' flesh; 'before Abraham came to be, I am'.

study.translationNote: μὴ γένοιτο is 'God forbid' in the KJV but 'By no means', 'Certainly not' or 'Absolutely not' in modern versions; the Greek has no word for God, and the KJV used the strongest English idiom of its day. Similarly 'And it came to pass' (KJV) for καὶ ἐγένετο is usually left untranslated or rendered 'when…' today.

background.note: The formula 'and it came to pass' (καὶ ἐγένετο) reproduces the Hebrew narrative connective וַיְהִי.
μὴ γένοιτο renders the Hebrew exclamation חָלִילָה, 'far be it!'.
ἐὰν γένηται + infinitive, 'if it should happen that', is common in letters, as in Acts.
γενόμενος with an official title means 'former', e.g. 'ex-strategus'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for contrast with εἰμί: where an author switches between 'was' and 'became/came to be' (JOH 1:1-14; JOH 8:58) the choice is often theologically deliberate.

study.summary: To make or to do: to create or produce something, to cause or bring about, to make someone into something, and to do, perform or practise actions, including obeying God's will.

senses.label: Make, create, produce
senses.definition: To bring something into existence or construct it; also to cause or bring about a state of affairs.
senses.note: Of God as creator; also 'make peace' (EPH 2:15; JAM 3:18), 'make purification' (HEB 1:3), 'cause divisions' (ROM 16:17).

senses.label: Make someone/something into
senses.definition: With a double accusative: to cause someone to be or become something, or to treat as such.
senses.note: 'We make him a liar' (1JO 1:10) = we treat God as a liar.

senses.label: Do, perform (deeds, signs)
senses.definition: To carry out an action or work, especially Jesus' mighty works and signs.
senses.note: With dative of person: do something to or for someone (MAR 5:19; MAT 7:12).

senses.label: Do, practise (God's will, law, truth)
senses.definition: To put a command or way of life into practice; to obey or to habitually practise good or evil.
senses.note: ποιεῖν τὸν νόμον = keep the law, not (as in classical Greek) make a law.

senses.label: Make (with noun): hold, take, prepare
senses.definition: With a noun of action, forming a phrase equivalent to a simple verb: make a journey, make one's home, prepare a meal, celebrate a feast, wage war.
senses.note: Often middle (ποιεῖσθαι) in this use.

senses.label: Spend (time)
senses.definition: With an expression of time: to spend or stay a period somewhere.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John speaks of 'doing the truth', and 1 John uses ποιεῖν τὴν δικαιοσύνην / τὴν ἁμαρτίαν (present tense) for a habitual way of life.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew stresses 'doing the will of the Father' as the mark of true discipleship.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Only Luke uses the Septuagintal phrase ποιεῖν ἔλεος / ποιεῖν μετά, 'to deal (mercifully) with'.

study.translationNote: In 1JO 3:9 ἁμαρτίαν οὐ ποιεῖ is 'doth not commit sin' (KJV) but 'does not keep on sinning' or 'makes a practice of sinning' (ESV, NIV), because many read the present tense as habitual. Translators differ on how much weight the tense can bear.

background.note: καλῶς / εὖ ποιήσεις + participle is the everyday letter idiom for 'please, kindly', as in 3JO 1:6.
ποιεῖν with an accusative of time means 'to spend' days somewhere, as in ACT 20:3 and JAM 4:13.
ποιεῖν (ἔλεος) μετά τινος, 'to act (kindly) toward', is common in the LXX and is echoed by Luke.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether ποιέω is creating (make), causing (make X into Y), or practising (do); when it governs a noun of action, translate with the matching verb (πορείαν ποιεῖσθαι = to travel).
study.caution: Some have argued that τοῦτο ποιεῖτε (LUK 22:19; 1CO 11:24) means 'offer this' in a sacrificial sense; most scholars read simply 'do this'. The habitual reading of present-tense ποιεῖν in 1 John is widely held but debated.

study.summary: A human being, whether male or female; humanity as distinct from God or animals; people in general; or a particular person. In Paul it also denotes the self, the 'old' and 'new' person.

senses.label: Human being, person
senses.definition: A member of the human race, without reference to sex; 'man' in the generic sense.
senses.note: Distinct from ἀνήρ, which normally means a male or husband.

senses.label: Merely human (vs God)
senses.definition: Humanity in contrast with God, or human standards and wisdom as opposed to divine.
senses.note: κατὰ ἄνθρωπον 'in a human way, by human standards' (ROM 3:5; 1CO 9:8; GAL 3:15).

senses.label: People, others (plural)
senses.definition: People in general, often 'other people' whose opinion or presence is in view.
senses.note: 'Before men' (MAT 6:1) = in front of other people.

senses.label: A certain person, someone
senses.definition: An individual, often indefinite ('a man', 'someone') or a particular person already mentioned.
senses.note: Hebraic characterizing phrases: 'man of God' (1TI 6:11; 2TI 3:17), 'man of lawlessness' (2TH 2:3).

senses.label: The self: inner, old, new
senses.definition: By extension, the human person viewed in its inner life or in its condition before and after union with Christ.
senses.note: esp. Paul; cf. 'the hidden person of the heart' (1PE 3:4).

senses.label: In the title 'Son of Man'
senses.definition: In ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Jesus' characteristic self-designation, drawing on Daniel 7.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew likes ἄνθρωπος joined to another noun, 'a man, a king', 'a man, a householder', in parables.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts the one man Adam with the one man Christ, and speaks of the 'old' and 'new' person.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the word with irony and depth: 'Behold the man!' and the Son of Man who must be 'lifted up'.

study.translationNote: Older versions render ἄνθρωπος 'man/men' throughout (KJV, NASB, NIV 1984); newer ones often use 'person, people, human being' (NRSV, NIV 2011, CSB). The Greek word is not male-specific, so gender-inclusive renderings are lexically justified where the context is generic; where a particular male is meant (MAT 9:9) 'man' remains correct.

background.note: From Homer on, mortals are set against the gods: 'the immortal gods and men who walk on the earth'.
A judge contrasts human and beast: 'you seem to have the soul of a beast, not of a human'.
The word can carry commiseration, 'I am an old man'.
Tobit sets ἄνθρωπος beside γυνή as if it meant 'male', a usage the NT avoids.

study.exegesisTip: In Paul, check whether ἄνθρωπος stands in contrast with God or the Spirit; 'human' then often means 'merely human' or 'by worldly standards' (1CO 3:3-4; GAL 1:11-12).
study.caution: The background and meaning of 'Son of Man' (a Danielic title, a self-reference, or an Aramaic idiom for 'a human being') is much debated. Scholars also differ on whether the 'old/new man' is an individual nature or the corporate humanity of Adam versus Christ.

study.summary: To hear: to perceive sound, to learn of something by report, to listen attentively, and, in the biblical sense of Hebrew shama', to heed and obey; also to understand, and (of God) to answer prayer.

senses.label: Hear, perceive sound
senses.definition: To perceive sounds or words with the ears; passive 'be heard'.

senses.label: Hear of, learn
senses.definition: To receive news or information about something by report.
senses.note: Often aorist participle ἀκούσας 'when he heard'.

senses.label: Listen, give a hearing
senses.definition: To pay attention to a speaker; also to hear a case judicially.
senses.note: 'He who has ears, let him hear' (MAT 11:15; REV 2:7).

senses.label: Heed, obey
senses.definition: To listen with acceptance and compliance, as reflected in Hebrew שָׁמַע 'hear/obey'.
senses.note: Often with the genitive: ἀκούειν τῆς φωνῆς 'listen to the voice'.

senses.label: Understand
senses.definition: To take in and grasp the meaning of what is said.
senses.note: 'Who can listen to it?' (JOH 6:60) = who can accept it?

senses.label: Hear prayer (of God)
senses.definition: Of God: to attend to and answer a request.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John hearing the Son's voice is the response of faith that brings life; Revelation repeats 'let him hear what the Spirit says'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul ties faith to hearing the preached word.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark's parable chapter is framed by commands to listen.

study.translationNote: ACT 9:7 says Paul's companions were 'hearing the voice' (genitive), while ACT 22:9 says they 'did not hear the voice' (accusative). KJV renders both with 'hear'; NIV renders 22:9 'did not understand the voice', following the view that the accusative means hearing with understanding. Whether the case difference really carries that distinction is disputed.

background.note: ἀκούειν τῆς φωνῆς reproduces the Hebrew idiom 'listen to the voice', meaning to obey.
Used of a judicial hearing, as when an official endorses a petition 'it will be heard', cf. ACT 25:22.
The imperative ἄκουε introduces an exposition, as in Jesus' 'Listen!' (MAR 4:3).

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the context requires mere perception or responsive obedience; in Jesus' calls to 'hear' and in the Shepherd discourse the latter is meant.
study.caution: The genitive/accusative distinction proposed to harmonize ACT 9:7 and 22:9 is debated; many grammarians think Koine usage does not consistently support it.

study.summary: Much, many, great: πολύς expresses large number, amount, degree or duration; its comparative πλείων ('more, the majority') and superlative πλεῖστος ('most, very great') belong to the same word.

senses.label: Many (number)
senses.definition: A large number of persons or things.

senses.label: Much, great (amount, degree)
senses.definition: A large quantity or high intensity of something, such as love, joy, endurance or zeal.
senses.note: 'Much wine' (1TI 3:8; TIT 2:3).

senses.label: Many people; 'the many'
senses.definition: As a noun: many people; with the article οἱ πολλοί, 'the many', which can be inclusive (= all, set against the one).
senses.note: Inclusive 'many' reflects Semitic idiom (cf. ISA 53:11-12).

senses.label: Long (of time)
senses.definition: Of time: a long period, or late in the day.

senses.label: Adverbial: much, greatly, often
senses.definition: Neuter forms used adverbially: much, greatly, earnestly, often; πολλῷ μᾶλλον 'much more'.
senses.note: πολλῷ μᾶλλον introduces an argument from lesser to greater (ROM 5:9; HEB 12:9).

senses.label: More, most (comparative, superlative)
senses.definition: πλείων: more, greater, the majority; πλεῖστος: most, very great.
senses.note: 'Something greater than Jonah is here' (MAT 12:41).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts 'the many' with 'the one' (Adam, Christ) and argues 'how much more' from lesser to greater.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark often uses adverbial πολλά, 'much, earnestly', for intensity.

study.translationNote: In MAR 10:45, MAT 26:28 and ROM 5:15-19 'for many' / 'the many' is kept by most versions, but commentators explain it as Semitic inclusive language meaning 'the multitude, all', not 'many but not all'; some paraphrases render it 'all'.

background.note: Common in letters, e.g. 'much thanks to the gods if you are well'.
πολλοῦ as genitive of price, 'very dear', as in MAT 26:9.
'Many' is a conventional word in literary prefaces, so 'many have undertaken' (LUK 1:1) should not be pressed.

study.exegesisTip: When οἱ πολλοί stands opposite 'the one' (ROM 5:15-19) or echoes Isaiah 53 (MAR 10:45), ask whether it means 'all' in Semitic fashion rather than 'a large number but not all'.
study.caution: How inclusive 'the many' is in MAR 10:45, MAT 26:28 and ROM 5 is debated; the Semitic 'many = all' argument is widely cited but not universally accepted.

study.summary: Father: a male parent or ancestor, a founder or respected elder, and above all God as Father of his people and, uniquely, of Jesus the Son.

senses.label: Male parent
senses.definition: A person's own father; in the plural occasionally both parents.
senses.note: οἱ πατέρες in HEB 11:23 = Moses' parents; οἱ τῆς σαρκὸς πατέρες (HEB 12:9) = earthly fathers.

senses.label: Ancestor, forefather
senses.definition: A remote progenitor, especially the patriarchs or earlier generations of Israel.
senses.note: Usually plural (οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν) for the forebears of the nation.

senses.label: Founder, spiritual originator
senses.definition: One who originates something or whose character others reproduce, as Abraham is father of all believers or the devil father of lies.
senses.note: A father is the source whose likeness his 'children' bear.

senses.label: Title of respect
senses.definition: Honorific address or designation for elders, teachers, or leaders of a community.
senses.note: Cf. OT usage for prophets and teachers; Jesus forbids its use as a religious title in MAT 23:9.

senses.label: God as Father of his people
senses.definition: God as the caring source and Lord of creation and especially of those in covenant relationship with him, who may address him as Father.
senses.note: Note 'Abba, Father' (ROM 8:15; GAL 4:6) and qualifying genitives: 'Father of mercies' (2CO 1:3), 'Father of lights' (JAM 1:17).

senses.label: God as Father of Jesus
senses.definition: God in his unique relationship to Jesus the Son, whether in Jesus' own speech ('my Father', 'the Father') or in apostolic confession.
senses.note: Formula 'the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' (ROM 15:6; 2CO 1:3; EPH 1:3).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses πατήρ more than any other NT author (about 160×), mostly of God in an absolute 'the Father' paired with 'the Son'; Jesus distinguishes 'my Father and your Father' rather than saying 'our Father' with the disciples.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew characteristically speaks of 'your/our Father in heaven' and 'your heavenly Father', framing discipleship as family life under a heavenly Father.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's greetings join 'God our Father' with 'the Lord Jesus Christ', and he grounds believers' adoption in the Spirit-prompted cry 'Abba, Father'.

study.translationNote: English versions capitalise 'Father' when God is meant, an editorial decision the Greek does not mark. The plural οἱ πατέρες is rendered 'fathers', 'forefathers' or 'ancestors' (e.g. NIV/NRSV 'ancestors'), and in HEB 11:23 'parents'.

background.note: From Homer onward the ordinary word for father; Zeus is called father of gods and men, a usage Abbott-Smith compares with God as Father.
Renders Hebrew 'āb, including as an honorific for prophets and teachers.
Used loosely as a title of respect for men other than one's real father.
A Christian woman addresses her spiritual father as 'my lord father', comparable to 1 Tim 5:1.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the possessive: 'my Father' (Jesus' unique sonship), 'your Father' (the disciples' relationship) and 'our Father' (the praying community) carry different nuances.
study.caution: The claim that Abba meant a childlike 'Daddy' (popularised by J. Jeremias) is widely judged overstated; Abba was also used by adults and conveys intimate yet respectful address.

study.summary: To give: hand over, grant or bestow, with wide idiomatic range (give one's life, appoint, permit, yield fruit) shaped by its object and context.

senses.label: Give, hand over
senses.definition: To transfer something physically into another's possession or use.

senses.label: Grant, bestow (gifts, authority)
senses.definition: To confer a non-material benefit such as authority, grace, knowledge or a throne, very often with God as giver.
senses.note: The passive (δοθήσεται, δέδοται) often implies God as the unnamed giver.

senses.label: Allow, permit (with infinitive)
senses.definition: To grant that someone may do or experience something; in the passive, 'it was granted/permitted'.
senses.note: Frequent in Revelation's ἐδόθη αὐτῷ, 'he was allowed'.

senses.label: Give oneself, one's life
senses.definition: To hand over oneself or one's life on behalf of others, especially of Christ's self-giving in death.
senses.note: Often with ὑπέρ or ἀντί; 2CO 8:5 of believers giving themselves to the Lord.

senses.label: Appoint, set, put
senses.definition: To place someone in a role or position, or put something in place (often with a double accusative).

senses.label: Idioms: give glory, account, effort
senses.definition: In fixed phrases δίδωμι means to render or produce: give glory, render an account, make an effort, give the right hand, yield fruit.
senses.note: Of seed 'yielding' fruit (MAR 4:7-8).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Fourth Gospel the Father 'gives' to the Son: all things, judgment, authority over all flesh, and the people who come to him; this giving defines the Son's mission.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation repeatedly uses the passive ἐδόθη, 'was given', for powers granted (even to hostile forces) under God's sovereign permission.

study.translationNote: Because δίδωμι is so general, versions vary its rendering by context: 'give', 'grant', 'allow', 'appoint', 'put', 'yield'. In Revelation's 'it was given to him' modern versions often write 'he was allowed/permitted', making explicit that the power is delegated.

background.note: The standard verb for giving from Homer onward.
The phrase δὸς ἐργασίαν, 'give your attention, make an effort', appears in a vernacular letter of 2 B.C., showing LUK 12:58 is ordinary Greek, not a Latinism.
An oracle question asks 'is it granted me (δέδοταί μοι) to marry?', illustrating the 'it is granted' idiom of MAT 19:11.
'We gave them Dorion as arbitrator' shows δίδωμι = appoint, as in ACT 13:20.

study.exegesisTip: When the verb is passive and no giver is named, ask whether God is the implied giver (a 'divine passive'), as in 'ask, and it will be given to you'.

study.summary: Wind, breath, spirit: the human spirit or inner self, a disposition, a spirit-being (good or evil), and above all the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit.

senses.label: Wind, breath
senses.definition: Moving air: the wind, or the breath of the mouth and of life.
senses.note: JOH 3:8 plays on wind and Spirit.

senses.label: Human spirit, life-principle
senses.definition: The inner, animating part of a person that departs at death, and the seat of inner awareness, emotion and will.
senses.note: Contrasted with σάρξ (MAT 26:41) or σῶμα; dative τῷ πνεύματι = 'in spirit' (MAT 5:3; MAR 8:12).

senses.label: Disposition, frame of mind
senses.definition: A prevailing attitude or spiritual state that characterises a person.
senses.note: Usually with a qualifying genitive: 'a spirit of gentleness', 'of fear', 'of slavery'.

senses.label: Spirit-being (non-evil)
senses.definition: An incorporeal being: God as spirit, angels, ghosts, or the spirits of the departed.

senses.label: Evil or unclean spirit
senses.definition: A demonic being that afflicts or possesses people.
senses.note: Often qualified as ἀκάθαρτον or πονηρόν.

senses.label: The Holy Spirit
senses.definition: The Spirit of God (and of Christ), God's own presence and power at work in creation, prophecy, Jesus' ministry and believers.
senses.note: Also 'Spirit of God', 'Spirit of Christ' (ROM 8:9), 'Spirit of truth' (JOH 15:26).

senses.label: Spirit versus letter and flesh
senses.definition: The new mode of existence created by God's Spirit, opposed to the written code (γράμμα) and to merely human 'flesh'.
senses.note: Esp. Paul; κατὰ πνεῦμα vs κατὰ σάρκα.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (149×) sets the Spirit against the flesh as two opposed powers or spheres of life, and makes the Spirit the mark and pledge of belonging to Christ.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents the Spirit chiefly as the Spirit of prophecy and mission: people are 'filled' with the Spirit and speak, and the Spirit directs the church's expansion.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John links Spirit with new birth and life, and in the farewell discourse calls him the 'Spirit of truth' sent by the Father and the Son.

study.translationNote: Greek manuscripts do not distinguish 'Spirit' from 'spirit', so capitalisation is an interpretive choice. Versions differ in passages such as ROM 1:4, ROM 12:11, 1CO 14:2 and 1PE 3:18, where the human spirit, Christ's spirit or the Holy Spirit may be meant. The KJV's 'Holy Ghost' is simply an older English equivalent of 'Holy Spirit'.

background.note: In classical Greek primarily a blast of wind or breath.
Literal 'breath of life': a petitioner says the very breath of his life is in danger.
A Jewish prayer for vengeance invokes God as 'Lord of the spirits and of all flesh', echoing Num 16:22.
A Christian prayer asks help for 'body, soul and spirit', paralleling the threefold phrase of 1 Thess 5:23.

study.exegesisTip: Look at what πνεῦμα is paired with or contrasted with (σάρξ, σῶμα, ψυχή, γράμμα) and how it is qualified (ἅγιον, θεοῦ, ἀκάθαρτον) to decide which sense is in play.
study.caution: The guideline that the article marks the Spirit as a person and its absence an influence or gift is only a tendency, not a rule. In several texts (e.g. ROM 1:4; 1PE 3:18; 1CO 5:5) scholars genuinely disagree whether the human spirit or the divine Spirit is meant.

study.summary: Son: a male child or descendant; idiomatically one who shares the character of something ('son of light'); and as titles, Son of God and Son of Man.

senses.label: Male child
senses.definition: A son born to a father or mother.

senses.label: Descendant, member of a people
senses.definition: A more remote descendant, or (plural) members of a nation: 'sons of Israel', 'son of David'.
senses.note: 'Son of David' functions as a messianic title (MAT 9:27; MAT 22:42).

senses.label: Characterised by, belonging to
senses.definition: With a genitive, one whose nature or destiny is defined by something: 'sons of light', 'sons of disobedience', 'son of encouragement'.
senses.note: A Semitic-flavoured idiom also found in Greek inscriptions.

senses.label: Sons of God (believers)
senses.definition: People who belong to God's family, reflect his character and share his inheritance.
senses.note: In Paul tied to adoption and heirship.

senses.label: Jesus as Son of God
senses.definition: Jesus in his unique relationship to God the Father, as messianic king and as the eternal Son.
senses.note: Absolute 'the Son' (MAT 11:27; JOH 3:35).

senses.label: Son of Man
senses.definition: Jesus' favoured self-designation, drawn from Dan 7:13, combining true humanity, humble mission, suffering and future glory.
senses.note: Almost only on Jesus' own lips; exceptions ACT 7:56; REV 1:13; REV 14:14.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews builds its Christology on the Son who is superior to angels and Moses, and uses the father-son bond for God's discipline of believers.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the absolute 'the Son' alongside 'the Father', stressing the Son's dependence on and unity with the Father and faith in the Son as the way to life.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links sonship with the Spirit, adoption and inheritance: those led by the Spirit are sons and therefore heirs.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew stresses Jesus as 'Son of David', the royal Messiah, from the first verse onward.

study.translationNote: Gender-inclusive versions (e.g. NRSV, NIV 2011) often render plural υἱοί 'children' ('children of God', MAT 5:9), while ESV and MSB keep 'sons', arguing that Paul's 'sons' carries the legal status of heirs. Idioms like 'sons of disobedience' are sometimes rendered 'those who are disobedient'.

background.note: Augustus is styled θεοῦ υἱός, 'son of god', in documents and inscriptions, giving the Christian title a pointed contemporary ring.
Honorific 'son of the city' shows the 'son of X' idiom is not purely Hebraistic.
Christian letters address a spiritual son as 'beloved son'.

study.exegesisTip: When υἱός is followed by an abstract genitive ('son of peace', 'son of perdition'), read it as describing character or destiny, not physical parentage.
study.caution: The background and meaning of 'Son of Man' are much debated: a title drawn from Daniel 7, an Aramaic idiom meaning 'a man' or 'I', or a deliberate combination of both.

study.summary: The numeral 'one': a single, only or united one; in Koine also 'a certain', distributive 'each', and in dates 'first'.

senses.label: One (numeral)
senses.definition: One as opposed to two or more.
senses.note: Often with partitive genitive or ἐκ: 'one of the prophets'.

senses.label: Only one, alone
senses.definition: One to the exclusion of all others, especially in confessing the one God.

senses.label: Not even one (emphatic)
senses.definition: With a negative, a stronger 'no one, none at all' than οὐδείς.
senses.note: οὐδὲ εἷς / ἓν ... οὐ μή.

senses.label: One and the same, united
senses.definition: Sharing a single identity, purpose or life; unity and concord.
senses.note: Neuter ἕν = one thing/entity; masculine εἷς = one person.

senses.label: A certain, a (indefinite)
senses.definition: With weakened force, equivalent to τις or an indefinite article.
senses.note: εἷς τις = 'a certain one'.

senses.label: Each; one ... another
senses.definition: Distributive and reciprocal uses: each one, one by one, one ... the other, one another.
senses.note: εἷς ἕκαστος; καθ᾽ εἷς; εἷς τὸν ἕνα = ἀλλήλους.

senses.label: First (in dates)
senses.definition: As an ordinal, 'first', especially 'the first day of the week'.
senses.note: μία τῶν σαββάτων, lit. 'one of the sabbaths'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul builds his theology of the church on 'one': one God, one Lord, one body, one Spirit, and believers made 'one' in Christ.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the neuter ἕν for the unity of Father and Son and the unity of believers that mirrors it.

study.translationNote: Versions render εἷς as 'one', 'a', 'a certain', 'each' or 'first' according to its function. 'The first day of the week' translates a Semitic-style idiom, literally 'one of the sabbaths'. In MAR 12:29 (the Shema) 'the Lord is one' is sometimes rendered 'the Lord alone'.

background.note: Renders Hebrew 'eḥad, including its indefinite use ('a ram').
εἷς as an ordinal in a date ('the twenty-first') is vernacular Greek.
εἷς = 'a certain' is attested in ordinary Greek without Semitic influence.
An inscription in Alexandria bears the acclamation Εἷς θεός, 'One God'.

study.exegesisTip: Check the gender: neuter ἕν in JOH 10:30 ('one thing') affirms unity without merging persons, while masculine εἷς in GAL 3:28 presents believers as 'one person' in Christ.
study.caution: Whether the indefinite and ordinal uses reflect Semitic influence or ordinary Koine development is debated; papyrus evidence shows both were current in vernacular Greek.

study.summary: Brother: a sibling, a fellow Israelite or neighbour, and most often in the NT a fellow believer in God's family.

senses.label: Blood brother
senses.definition: A male sibling sharing one or both parents.

senses.label: Jesus' brothers
senses.definition: The 'brothers of the Lord', members of Jesus' family named in the Gospels and early church.
senses.note: See caution on their precise relationship.

senses.label: Fellow Israelite, kinsman
senses.definition: A member of the same nation or people.
senses.note: Address ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί to Jewish audiences.

senses.label: Neighbour, fellow member
senses.definition: Another person in one's community, the one toward whom one has obligations.
senses.note: In Jesus' teaching, especially a fellow disciple.

senses.label: Fellow believer
senses.definition: A member of the Christian community, God's family, whether named individually or addressed collectively.
senses.note: The vocative plural ἀδελφοί addresses whole congregations, women included.

senses.label: Christ's brothers
senses.definition: Believers as the brothers of the risen Christ, sharing his sonship.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul's letters account for 134 uses: he constantly addresses congregations as 'brothers' and names co-workers as 'the brother'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: 1 John makes love or hatred of one's 'brother' the test of being in the light and having passed from death to life.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James repeatedly appeals to 'my (beloved) brothers', giving his exhortations a pastoral, familial tone.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί when Jewish speakers address fellow Jews.

study.translationNote: When ἀδελφοί addresses a whole congregation, versions such as NRSV and NIV 2011 write 'brothers and sisters', while ESV and MSB keep 'brothers' (often with a footnote). The Greek masculine plural can include women, as classical usage shows, so the choice is about English style, not about who is addressed.

background.note: The plural ἀδελφοί could mean 'brother and sister'.
Renders Hebrew 'āḥ, used for a neighbour and for a fellow Israelite.
Members of a pagan religious guild call each other 'brothers', illustrating the term for a religious community.
Christian letters address a presbyter as 'beloved brother in the Lord'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide which family circle is in view (household, nation, or church), since the same word moves between them, sometimes in one passage (MAT 12:46-50).
study.caution: Whether Jesus' 'brothers' were sons of Joseph and Mary, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or cousins is debated along confessional lines; Abbott-Smith notes that the cousin view does not fit normal Greek usage of ἀδελφός.

study.summary: Word: a saying or message, speech, the word of God or gospel, a matter or report, an account or reckoning, a reason; in John, the divine Word who became flesh.

senses.label: Word, saying
senses.definition: A spoken word or statement that expresses a thought, including commands and teachings.

senses.label: Speech, manner of speaking
senses.definition: The act or style of speaking, discourse, or eloquence, sometimes contrasted with deed or power.
senses.note: λόγος vs δύναμις (1CO 4:19-20); vs ἔργον (ROM 15:18).

senses.label: The message, word of God
senses.definition: God's message, especially the gospel, as preached, received and obeyed.
senses.note: Often absolute 'the word'; also 'the word of the cross' (1CO 1:18).

senses.label: Matter, report, story
senses.definition: The thing talked about: an affair, a case at law, or a report or story that spreads.

senses.label: Account, reckoning
senses.definition: A financial or moral account that must be rendered, as before a master or before God.
senses.note: Commercial sense 'credit, account' in PHP 4:15-17.

senses.label: Reason, ground
senses.definition: A cause or ground for doing something.
senses.note: παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας, 'except on the ground of sexual immorality'.

senses.label: The Word (Christ)
senses.definition: The divine Word who was with God and was God, became flesh in Jesus, and is the expression of God himself.
senses.note: Only in the Johannine writings.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Besides the unique Logos title of the prologue, John speaks of 'keeping' Jesus' word as the mark of a true disciple.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents 'the word of God' almost as an actor that spreads, grows and multiplies with the church's mission.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews plays on λόγος: the living word of God that judges, and the God 'to whom we must give account'.

study.translationNote: English uses many words for λόγος: 'word', 'message', 'saying', 'speech', 'account', 'matter', 'reason'. In JOH 1:1 versions capitalise 'Word' to show it names a person; in 1PE 3:15 some render 'reason' and others 'account' or 'defense' for the λόγος believers are asked for.

background.note: From early prose λόγος also meant computation or an account of money handled.
Renders Hebrew dābār; in the plural it can mean 'affairs, matters', as in LUK 1:4.
Very common in business documents for an account: payment 'to the account of maintenance'.
Legal sense 'matter in dispute, lawsuit', as in ACT 19:38.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether λόγος points to what is said (message), the act of saying (speech), or a reckoning (account); a following genitive (of God, of the cross, of truth) often settles it.
study.caution: The background of John's Logos is debated: Greek philosophy (Stoic reason, Philo's Logos), the creative word of Genesis 1, and Jewish Wisdom traditions have all been proposed; most see John drawing mainly on the Old Testament while speaking in terms Greek readers would recognise.

study.summary: To know (perfect οἶδα with present meaning): to know a fact, be acquainted with a person, know how to do something, and occasionally to understand or respect.

senses.label: Know a fact
senses.definition: To have knowledge that something is so, or to know what, who or when.
senses.note: Very often with ὅτι or an indirect question.

senses.label: Know a person
senses.definition: To be acquainted with, recognise or have a relationship with someone, including knowing God.
senses.note: 'I do not know you' (MAT 25:12) denies relationship, not information.

senses.label: Know how to
senses.definition: With an infinitive, to have the skill or capacity to do something.

senses.label: Understand
senses.definition: To grasp the meaning of something said.

senses.label: Respect, acknowledge
senses.definition: To recognise someone's worth and give them due regard.
senses.note: A rare, distinctive use.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul often appeals to shared knowledge with 'we know that' or 'do you not know that...?', reminding readers of truths they should already grasp.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses Jesus' sure knowledge of his origin, destiny and the Father, and in 1 John the believers' confident 'we know'.

study.translationNote: Usually rendered 'know', but versions shift to 'understand' (JOH 16:18; 1CO 11:3), 'recognise', or 'respect' (1TH 5:12) according to context. In 1TH 4:4 'know how to control' and 'learn to control' reflect different readings of the infinitive.

background.note: The related aorist εἶδον 'saw' appears in a Decian-era certificate of sacrifice: 'we saw you sacrificing'; the root originally meant 'see', and οἶδα is literally 'I have seen', hence 'I know'.

study.exegesisTip: When Paul writes 'do you not know that...?', treat what follows as foundational teaching he assumes, and the question as a rebuke for not living by it.
study.caution: The common claim that οἶδα means intuitive, settled knowledge while γινώσκω means knowledge gained by experience has some basis but is often overpressed; in Koine the two overlap heavily (e.g. JOH 21:17 uses both).

study.summary: To speak: utter words, talk with someone, tell or proclaim a message; used of human speech, of God's revelation, and even of things that 'speak'.

senses.label: Speak, have speech
senses.definition: To use the faculty of speech, especially of the mute who are healed.
senses.note: Absolute use, stressing the act of speaking.

senses.label: Talk, converse
senses.definition: To talk with or to someone.
senses.note: With dative or πρός / μετά.

senses.label: Tell, proclaim a message
senses.definition: To communicate content, especially to preach or declare the word.
senses.note: λαλεῖν τὸν λόγον, 'speak the word' = preach.

senses.label: God speaking, revealing
senses.definition: Of God (or the Spirit) communicating his will, through prophets and finally through the Son.

senses.label: Inspired or ecstatic speech
senses.definition: Speaking in tongues or prophesying under the Spirit's prompting.
senses.note: λαλεῖν γλώσσαις.

senses.label: Figurative utterance
senses.definition: Of a voice, thunder, or a person's blood or example that 'speaks'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, Jesus speaks only what he has heard from the Father, so his speaking is the Father's own word.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews opens and closes its argument with the God who has spoken, warning readers not to refuse him who speaks.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: 1 Corinthians 14 uses λαλέω repeatedly for speaking in tongues and prophesying in the assembly.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses 'speaking the word' for the bold proclamation of the gospel.

study.translationNote: Versions render λαλέω 'speak', 'talk', 'tell', 'say' or 'preach'. Unlike λέγω, which highlights what is said, λαλέω highlights the act of speaking, so it often stands without an object; in phrases like 'he spoke to them, saying' both verbs appear together.

background.note: In classical Attic λαλέω often meant 'chatter, prattle', contrasted with λέγω 'speak to the point'.
A comic poet mocks one who is 'best at chattering, most incapable of speaking'.
A boy threatens his father: 'I won't write you a letter or speak to you', showing everyday use for talking.

study.exegesisTip: Note whether λαλέω has an object: absolute use draws attention to the act of speaking (a mute man speaks), while with an object (the word, parables) it is proclamation.
study.caution: Some argue that the prohibition on women 'speaking' in 1CO 14:34 reflects the classical sense 'chatter', but NT usage of λαλέω is generally dignified, so the precise sense there remains debated.

study.summary: Heaven: the visible sky; heaven and earth as the whole creation; the dwelling of God, angels and the exalted Christ; and by reverent metonymy, God himself.

senses.label: Sky, the heavens above
senses.definition: The visible sky with its clouds, stars and birds; the atmosphere.
senses.note: 'Birds of the air' = birds of the sky.

senses.label: Heaven and earth: the universe
senses.definition: Paired with earth, the whole created order.
senses.note: Its passing away and renewal (2PE 3:10; REV 21:1).

senses.label: God's dwelling place
senses.definition: The realm where God reigns, angels serve and the risen Christ is exalted, from which revelation, salvation and judgment come.
senses.note: Also where believers' reward and citizenship are kept (MAT 6:20; PHP 3:20).

senses.label: Heaven opened: revelation
senses.definition: Heaven opening as a sign of divine revelation or intervention.

senses.label: Heaven = God (reverent substitute)
senses.definition: Used in place of God's name, as was common in Jewish speech.
senses.note: 'Kingdom of heaven' = 'kingdom of God'.

senses.label: Inhabitants of heaven
senses.definition: By metonymy, those who dwell in heaven.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew alone speaks of 'the kingdom of heaven' (plural τῶν οὐρανῶν) and favours 'your Father in heaven'; he uses οὐρανός more than any other NT writer.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews portrays Christ passing through the heavens and entering heaven itself as high priest.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul speaks of a plurality of heavens (the 'third heaven'), Christ ascended above them, and believers' citizenship there.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel stresses Jesus as the one who came down from heaven; Revelation shows heaven opened and a new heaven and earth.

study.translationNote: The NT often uses the plural οὐρανοί, reflecting Hebrew šāmayim, but English versions usually write singular 'heaven'. Translators must choose between 'sky' and 'heaven' (e.g. ACT 1:11 has both in MSB), and 'kingdom of heaven' is retained in Matthew though it means the same as 'kingdom of God'.

background.note: In Homer and Hesiod the vault or firmament of the sky; classical writers never use the plural.
Renders Hebrew šāmayim; the heavens are called on to rejoice, personifying their inhabitants.
A later text invokes powers seated in the first, second and third heaven, illustrating the idea of several heavens (2 Cor 12:2).
A Christian letter echoes PHP 3:20: 'your citizenship in heaven'.

study.exegesisTip: In Matthew, read 'kingdom of heaven' as God's reign breaking into the world, not primarily as a place people go after death.
study.caution: Scholars debate whether Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven' is only a reverent substitute for 'God' or also a deliberate contrast between heaven and earth that runs through his Gospel.

study.summary: A learner or pupil attached to a teacher. In the Gospels it is mainly someone who follows Jesus, often the Twelve; in Acts it becomes a normal name for any Christian.

senses.label: Pupil of a teacher
senses.definition: One who learns from and follows a particular teacher or school, the counterpart of 'teacher' (διδάσκαλος).
senses.note: Usually with a genitive of the teacher: disciples of John, of the Pharisees, of Moses.

senses.label: Follower of Jesus
senses.definition: Anyone who attached himself or herself to Jesus as teacher during his ministry, a circle wider than the Twelve.
senses.note: This wider group can include half-committed followers who later turn away (JOH 6:66).

senses.label: The Twelve
senses.definition: The inner group Jesus chose and trained, often simply called 'the disciples' or 'his disciples'.
senses.note: Context decides whether 'the disciples' means the Twelve or the wider group.

senses.label: Christian believer
senses.definition: After Easter, a standard term for members of the Christian community, believers in Jesus as Lord.
senses.note: Found only in the Gospels and Acts; the letters use other terms such as 'brothers' or 'saints'.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses 'the disciples' as a plain name for the church's members, the name that preceded 'Christians' at Antioch.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses what makes a true disciple: remaining in Jesus' word, love for one another, bearing fruit. He also notes disciples who fell away, and 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'.

background.note: Common in Attic Greek for the pupils of philosophers and rhetoricians, such as the followers of Protagoras.
In the papyri it can mean an apprentice in a trade; hieroglyph-carvers swear they have no apprentices practising the craft.
Practically absent from the Septuagint, found only as a textual variant in Jeremiah, so the NT usage does not grow out of Greek OT vocabulary.

study.exegesisTip: A μαθητής is always someone's disciple; note whose disciple is meant and whether 'the disciples' refers to the Twelve or to a wider circle of followers.
study.caution: In ACT 19:1 Paul meets 'disciples' at Ephesus who knew only John's baptism; interpreters disagree whether Luke regards them as Christians or as followers of John the Baptist.

study.summary: A very common verb covering both actively taking something and passively receiving what is given. Context decides whether someone takes, seizes, takes on, receives or accepts.

senses.label: Take in hand
senses.definition: To take hold of an object physically, often as the first step of an action.
senses.note: The participle λαβών often just sets up the main verb ('took the loaves and blessed').

senses.label: Seize, take by force
senses.definition: To take hold of someone or something against their will, or take away what belongs to another.

senses.label: Take on, assume
senses.definition: To take something upon oneself, such as a role, a form, an honour, or another's burden; also idioms such as 'take a wife'.

senses.label: Receive, obtain
senses.definition: To get what is given or comes to one, whether goods, payment, power, gifts or reward.
senses.note: Often paired with asking or giving (MAT 7:8; MAT 10:8).

senses.label: Accept, welcome
senses.definition: To receive a message, testimony or person with approval, accepting it as true or welcoming them.

senses.label: Show partiality (idiom)
senses.definition: In the Hebrew-style phrase 'receive the face' (πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν), to favour someone because of their status.
senses.note: Reflects the Hebrew idiom nasa panim.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In John, 'receiving' Jesus or his testimony is a way of describing faith; refusing to receive him is unbelief.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the verb for what believers receive from God (grace, the Spirit, reconciliation), stressing that everything is a gift.

study.translationNote: Because the Greek verb covers both 'take' and 'receive', English versions often divide between them. The same form can be rendered 'take', 'receive' or 'accept' (e.g. REV 22:17, 'take' or 'receive' the water of life). The choice depends on whether the subject is acting or being given something.

background.note: Very common for receiving letters and documents: 'on receipt of this document, act in accordance with it'.
Standard in money and goods receipts ('we have received from you…').
Legal phrase λαμβάνειν τὸ δίκαιον, 'obtain satisfaction' in a lawsuit.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the subject actively takes something or receives it as a gift; in passages about grace, the Spirit and spiritual gifts the receptive sense governs (1CO 4:7).

study.summary: The earth, either the whole world as opposed to heaven or sea, or a particular land, region or country. It can also mean soil or the ground underfoot.

senses.label: Earth as opposed to heaven
senses.definition: The created world below, in contrast with heaven, the realm of God.
senses.note: Often in the pair 'heaven and earth' or 'in heaven and on earth'.

senses.label: The world and its people
senses.definition: The whole inhabited earth, sometimes standing for the people who live on it.

senses.label: Dry land
senses.definition: Land as opposed to sea or water.

senses.label: Soil
senses.definition: Earth as ground that can be farmed and bears crops.

senses.label: The ground
senses.definition: The surface underfoot, onto which things fall or people sit or bow.

senses.label: Land, country, region
senses.definition: A particular territory, often named ('land of Israel', 'land of Judah', 'land of Egypt').

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Most of John's uses are in Revelation, where earth, sea and heaven are the stage of God's judgments and 'those who dwell on the earth' are humanity hostile to God.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews contrasts the earthly land of promise, where the patriarchs lived as strangers, with the heavenly homeland they looked for.

study.translationNote: Translations choose between 'earth' and 'land' depending on whether they judge the scope to be worldwide or local. For example, MAT 27:45 is rendered 'darkness over all the land' or 'over all the earth', and JAM 5:17 'on the land' or 'on the earth'.

background.note: From early Greek on, γῆ is the earth including land and sea, and its pairing with heaven is ancient.
In the papyri γῆ usually means a plot of land, even in the plural; Moulton–Milligan note that this sense never occurs in the NT.
The biblical phrase ἐπὶ γῆς appears in a surveyor's report meaning 'on the spot'.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the contrasting term: 'heaven' points to the earth as a whole, 'sea' to dry land, a place-name to a country; this usually settles 'earth' or 'land'.
study.caution: In MAT 5:5 ('the meek will inherit the earth/land') the wording echoes PSA 37:11, about Israel's land. Scholars debate whether Jesus means the land of promise or a renewed whole earth.

study.summary: To answer or reply. In the Gospels it often means simply 'responded' or 'spoke up' to a situation, especially in the Hebrew-style formula 'answered and said', even when no question was asked.

senses.label: Answer a question
senses.definition: To give a reply to a question or statement addressed to one.
senses.note: Usually with the dative of the person answered; often ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν, 'answered and said'.

senses.label: Respond, speak up
senses.definition: Following Hebrew usage (ʿanah), to react to a situation or begin to speak without having been asked anything.
senses.note: Frequently redundant with a verb of saying (MAT 4:4; MAR 3:33).

senses.label: Answer a charge
senses.definition: To reply to accusations in a hearing or trial, or pointedly to give no answer.
senses.note: The middle aorist ἀπεκρίνατο in Jesus' trial scenes matches its use for legal replies in the papyri.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb most of all, often in the pattern 'Jesus answered and said to him', marking the back-and-forth of his long dialogues.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul has the verb only once, of giving a gracious answer to outsiders.

study.translationNote: Versions render the same Greek as 'answered', 'replied', 'said' or even 'declared'. Where no question has been asked (e.g. MAT 11:25), many modern versions avoid 'answered' because the Greek is a Hebrew-style way of introducing a response, not necessarily a reply.

background.note: In non-literary papyri the middle aorist ἀπεκρίνατο is found almost only in legal reports, where an advocate or party 'replied' in court.
The older active ἀποκρίνω meant 'separate, distinguish'; an inscription uses it in the passive of territory 'set apart'.
The passive aorist ἀπεκρίθη, the most common NT form, is surprisingly rare in non-literary Koine, its early examples being mainly inscriptions, some of them Roman senatorial decrees.

study.exegesisTip: When no one has asked a question, read ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν as 'responded' or 'spoke up' and ask what in the scene the speaker is reacting to.

study.summary: To believe or trust: to accept something as true, to believe a person, or to put one's trust in God or Christ. It can also mean 'entrust', and in the passive 'be entrusted with'.

senses.label: Believe something is true
senses.definition: To accept a statement or fact as true; often with ὅτι ('believe that…') or a neuter object.

senses.label: Believe a person
senses.definition: With the dative, to give credence to a person or their words, treating what they say as reliable.

senses.label: Trust in, rely on
senses.definition: To put personal trust in God or Christ, committing oneself to him; typically with εἰς, ἐπί or ἐν.
senses.note: 'Believe in the gospel' (MAR 1:15) uses ἐν.

senses.label: Have faith; be a believer
senses.definition: Used without an object for exercising faith, or (as a participle, 'those who believe') for Christians as a group.

senses.label: Entrust
senses.definition: With accusative and dative, to commit something or oneself to someone's care.

senses.label: Be entrusted with
senses.definition: In the passive, to be given something as a trust, such as the gospel or God's oracles.
senses.note: esp. Paul, of his commission.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb about 100 times but never the noun 'faith' in his Gospel. He prefers 'believe into' (εἰς) and writes so that readers may believe (JOH 20:31). He also shows inadequate believing: Jesus does not 'entrust' himself to those who believed only because of signs.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: For Paul, believing is how a person is justified, apart from works, and it is open to Jew and Greek alike.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James points out that even demons 'believe' that God is one; belief as mere assent, without deeds, does not save.

study.translationNote: Almost always rendered 'believe'. English has no verb related to 'faith', so the link between πιστεύω and πίστις is hidden. 'Believe' can also sound like mere opinion, when the Greek often means personal trust. At JOH 2:24 the same verb is rendered 'entrust', a play on 'believed' in 2:23.

background.note: From Herodotus on it means to trust or rely on a person, thing or statement.
The LXX already uses πιστεύω with ἐν for trusting in God, the background to NT 'believe in'.
Everyday letters use it for trusting someone with a task: 'I have trusted no one to take it to her'.
A Delphic manumission says a slave-woman 'entrusted' her purchase price to Apollo, illustrating the 'entrust' sense.

study.exegesisTip: Note the construction: dative (believe someone), ὅτι (believe a fact), or εἰς/ἐπί/ἐν (put one's trust in a person). It helps show what kind of believing is in view.
study.caution: Grammarians caution against pressing the constructions too hard: John uses dative and εἰς with overlapping force, and those who 'believed in him' (JOH 8:30) are addressed as having 'believed him' (8:31) before turning hostile.

study.summary: Faith or trust, especially in God or Christ; also faithfulness or reliability, 'the faith' as the content of Christian belief, and sometimes a pledge or proof.

senses.label: Trust in God or Christ
senses.definition: Confident reliance on God or Christ and his power and promises; in the Gospels often the faith that brings healing.
senses.note: The object can be a genitive ('faith of God' = in God, MAR 11:22) or follow εἰς, ἐν, πρός or ἐπί.

senses.label: Faithfulness, reliability
senses.definition: The quality of being trustworthy and loyal, said of people and of God himself.

senses.label: Personal conviction
senses.definition: One's settled conviction about what is permissible before God, which governs conscience.

senses.label: The faith (body of belief)
senses.definition: What is believed: the Christian message or teaching held by the church.
senses.note: Often with the article; esp. Acts, Jude and the Pastoral Letters.

senses.label: Pledge, proof
senses.definition: A guarantee that gives grounds for belief, or a pledge of loyalty given.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the noun more than all other writers combined, setting faith against 'works of the law' as the way of being right with God.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: In Hebrews, faith is forward-looking and enduring: confidence in what is hoped for and unseen, shown in steadfastness.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James attacks a faith that produces no deeds, calling it dead. He means a bare profession, not the active trust Paul commends.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Gospel never uses the noun; it appears only in 1 John and Revelation, where it means faithful perseverance.

study.translationNote: Most versions render 'faith' nearly everywhere, but some use 'faithfulness' where reliability is meant (GAL 5:22; ROM 3:3). The phrase πίστις Χριστοῦ is rendered 'faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ' depending on how translators read the genitive.

background.note: From Hesiod on it means trust placed in others.
Common for faithfulness or loyalty: a woman 'showing entire faithfulness towards me'.
An inscription says 'I kept the faith' (τὴν πίστιν ἐτήρησα), the same phrase as 2 Tim 4:7.
background.citation: Brit. Mus. Inscrr. Part III. No. 587

background.note: In business documents πίστις can mean a bond or security for a debt.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether πίστις refers to the act of trusting, the quality of being trustworthy, or the content believed. Articles and genitives often decide it, e.g. 'the faith(fulness) of God' in ROM 3:3.
study.caution: The phrase πίστις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (ROM 3:22; ROM 3:26; GAL 2:16; GAL 2:20; PHP 3:9) is debated. It may mean believers' faith in Christ (objective genitive) or Christ's own faith or faithfulness (subjective genitive). Both readings have strong scholarly support.

study.summary: Holy: belonging to God and set apart for him, and sharing his purity. It describes God himself, the Holy Spirit, sacred things and places, Christ, and God's people ('the saints').

senses.label: Holy as God is holy
senses.definition: God's own character: his majesty, purity and otherness that call for reverence.

senses.label: The Holy Spirit
senses.definition: In the phrase πνεῦμα ἅγιον, the Spirit of God; the word's most frequent NT use.

senses.label: Sacred things and places
senses.definition: Objects, places or writings set apart for God, such as the temple, the holy city, the Scriptures and the law.
senses.note: The neuter (τὸ ἅγιον, τὰ ἅγια) can mean the sanctuary itself.

senses.label: Consecrated persons
senses.definition: Persons set apart for God's service: Christ as 'the Holy One', angels and prophets.

senses.label: Saints, God's people
senses.definition: As a plural noun (οἱ ἅγιοι), believers as a people consecrated to God, not an elite among them.

senses.label: Morally pure
senses.definition: Holy in conduct: living in a way that matches belonging to God.
senses.note: Often paired with 'blameless' (ἄμωμος).

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul regularly addresses whole congregations as 'saints', calling all believers holy by God's call, whatever their behaviour.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews uses the neuter plural for the tabernacle's holy place and holy of holies, and for the heavenly sanctuary Christ entered.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke speaks of the Holy Spirit more than any other Gospel writer, from the birth narratives to the church's mission.

study.translationNote: The same adjective is rendered 'holy' or, as a plural noun, 'saints'. Modern English 'saints' suggests exceptionally virtuous Christians, but the Greek means 'holy ones', all of God's consecrated people. Some versions therefore use 'God's people' or 'holy ones'. Older versions say 'Holy Ghost' for πνεῦμα ἅγιον.

background.note: In Herodotus ἅγιος describes temples and sacred precincts; it is rare in Attic and absent from Homer and tragedy.
The LXX uses it chiefly for Hebrew qodesh/qadosh, including τὸ ἅγιον for the sanctuary.
Inscriptions use it as a title of pagan deities, e.g. 'to the holy most high god'.
The oldest recovered Christian letter uses the superlative 'most holy' of church leaders.

study.exegesisTip: Ask 'set apart to whom, and for what?' ἅγιος is first about belonging to God and only then about the conduct that belonging requires.
study.caution: Some uses are debated: in 1TH 3:13 Jesus comes 'with all his holy ones', who may be angels or believers. In 1CO 7:14 the children of a believer are called 'holy', and what that status means is disputed.

study.summary: Great or large, in size, intensity or importance; with 'voice' it means loud. The comparative μείζων ('greater') often serves as a superlative ('greatest').

senses.label: Large in size
senses.definition: Physically big or extensive: a stone, a city, a fish, branches, a dragon.

senses.label: Intense, strong
senses.definition: Great in degree: strong feelings, violent storms, severe fever, heavy distress.

senses.label: Loud
senses.definition: With 'voice' or 'cry', a loud sound.
senses.note: Usually φωνῇ μεγάλῃ, 'with a loud voice'.

senses.label: Important, eminent
senses.definition: Great in rank, significance or dignity, of persons, days, events or truths.
senses.note: 'Small and great' covers everyone, low and high (ACT 8:10).

senses.label: Greater, greatest
senses.definition: Comparative forms (μείζων, double comparative μειζότερος) meaning 'greater', often with superlative force 'greatest'.
senses.note: Even the positive can serve as a superlative: 'which is the great (= greatest) commandment' (MAT 22:36).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: Revelation uses μέγας constantly: loud voices, a great city (Babylon), the great day of wrath. In the Gospel and letters, comparatives make Christological claims ('greater things', 'the Father is greater than I', 'greater is he who is in you').

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke highlights the disciples' dispute over who is 'greatest' and Jesus' reversal: the greatest must become like the youngest and the servant.

study.translationNote: English needs different words for the one Greek adjective: 'great', 'large', 'loud', 'strong'. Because Koine often uses the comparative for the superlative, versions differ between 'greater' and 'greatest' (1CO 13:13; MAT 18:1) and between 'great' and 'greatest' commandment (MAT 22:36).

background.note: From Homer on it means big, especially of bodily stature.
A frequent title of pagan deities ('great Isis'), like 'great is Artemis of the Ephesians' (Acts 19:28).
Used after a name to mark the elder of two people with the same name, like English 'senior'.
Doubled ('great great god') as an emphatic superlative in an oracle question.

study.exegesisTip: Let the noun guide the sense: with 'voice' it means loud, with objects large, with emotions intense, with persons or events important.
