senses.definition: A condition that must be met to enter life or please God.

senses.label: Moral obligation, ought
senses.definition: What is right and fitting, a duty one ought to fulfil; negated, 'must not'.
senses.note: οὐ δεῖ 'must not' (2TI 2:24; ACT 25:24).

senses.label: What should have been (ἔδει)
senses.definition: The imperfect ἔδει of an obligation in the past, often one not met: 'you ought to have'.

senses.label: Practical necessity
senses.definition: What circumstances require or make unavoidable.
senses.note: Often the line between practical and divine necessity is thin (JOH 4:4).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke (43 uses) makes δεῖ a key word for the plan of God: Jesus 'must' be in his Father's house, preach, suffer and rise, and the gospel 'must' go on to Rome.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John links δεῖ with the Son of Man 'lifted up', with new birth, and with Jesus' mission; Revelation uses it of what 'must soon take place'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses it of eschatological necessity and of what fits Christian conduct and church leaders.

study.translationNote: English 'must', 'had to', 'ought', 'should' and 'it is necessary' all render δεῖ, so readers cannot tell whether the necessity is God's plan, a moral duty or mere circumstance. JOH 4:4 'he had to pass through Samaria' is a classic example.

background.note: Originally 'there is need'; the sense of moral obligation, properly belonging to χρή, appears later in classical usage.
Everyday necessity: 'even if you have to pawn your cloak'.
Past obligation with ἔδει: 'you oughtn't even to have needed a reminder'.

study.exegesisTip: Ask who or what imposes the necessity: God's plan and Scripture, a moral duty, the end-time programme, or practical circumstances.
study.caution: Whether JOH 4:4 ('he had to go through Samaria') states geographical convenience or divine necessity is debated; Samaria could be bypassed, which leads many to see God's purpose.

study.summary: To lift or raise up; to pick up and carry; to take away or remove; and by extension to do away with someone, or (of Christ) to take away sin.

senses.label: Lift up, raise
senses.definition: To raise something upward: a stone, the eyes, the voice, the hand.
senses.note: Idioms: 'lift up the voice' (ACT 4:24), 'raise the hand' in an oath (REV 10:5); JOH 10:24 'how long will you keep us in suspense?' (literally 'lift our soul').

senses.label: Pick up and carry
senses.definition: To take something up and bear it along, such as a mat, provisions or leftovers.

senses.label: Take up the cross / yoke
senses.definition: To shoulder a burden willingly; of discipleship as bearing the cross after Jesus, or taking his yoke.
senses.note: Literal in MAR 15:21 (Simon of Cyrene), figurative in the discipleship sayings.

senses.label: Take away, remove
senses.definition: To carry something off or take it away from someone, often as judgment or loss.
senses.note: Of moving a mountain: 'be taken up and thrown into the sea' (MAT 21:21).

senses.label: Take away sin
senses.definition: Of Christ removing sin or the record of debt, putting it out of the way.
senses.note: Behind it stands Hebrew nāśāʾ, which can mean both 'bear' and 'take away' sin.

senses.label: Do away with, kill
senses.definition: To remove someone by death; the crowd's cry 'away with him!'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (29 uses) uses αἴρω at key points: the Lamb who takes away the world's sin, the life no one takes from Jesus, and the body 'taken away' from the tomb.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: The Synoptic call to 'take up the cross' is first in Mark, who also tells of Simon carrying Jesus' cross.

study.translationNote: In JOH 1:29 most versions read 'takes away', while some (and many margins) read 'bears', reflecting the Hebrew idea of bearing sin. In JOH 15:2 'takes away' (most) versus 'lifts up' (some commentators and paraphrases) changes the picture of the unfruitful branch.

background.note: A schoolboy's letter has his mother say 'he upsets me: away with him!', the same cry as JOH 19:15.
A legal text says 'remove these things from the midst', a close parallel to COL 2:14.
A children's alphabet uses αἴρειν for stealing a garment, 'carrying off'.
An inscription prays with 'raised hands' for vengeance, as in REV 10:5's lifted hand.

study.exegesisTip: Check the object and any preposition: lifting something up, carrying it, or taking it away (ἀπό, ἐκ) are different actions with the same verb.
study.caution: In JOH 15:2 some argue αἴρει means 'lifts up' (tends) the fruitless branch rather than 'takes away' (removes) it; most lexicons and versions favour removal.

study.summary: Good: of high quality and beneficial, morally upright, kind and generous; as a noun, what is good and right, someone's benefit, and good things or blessings.

senses.label: Good in quality, beneficial
senses.definition: Sound, excellent of its kind and beneficial to those who receive it: good trees, soil, gifts, hearts, conscience.
senses.note: 'Good conscience' (ACT 23:1; 1PE 3:16), 'good hope' (2TH 2:16).

senses.label: Morally good (persons)
senses.definition: Upright and virtuous in character, often paired with faithful or contrasted with evil.
senses.note: Opposite πονηρός (MAT 5:45).

senses.label: God's goodness
senses.definition: The absolute goodness belonging to God alone.

senses.label: Kind, generous
senses.definition: Benevolent and kindly, showing goodness towards others.
senses.note: In ROM 5:7 the 'good' man (benefactor) seems to be set beside the merely 'righteous'.

senses.label: What is good and right
senses.definition: As a noun (τὸ ἀγαθόν), what is morally good and pleasing to God, which one does, pursues and clings to.
senses.note: 'Good work(s)' (ἔργον ἀγαθόν): EPH 2:10; PHP 1:6; COL 1:10.

senses.label: Someone's good, benefit
senses.definition: What serves a person's welfare or advantage.
senses.note: εἰς ἀγαθόν 'for good' (ROM 8:28).

senses.label: Good things, goods, blessings
senses.definition: Plural τὰ ἀγαθά: material possessions and comforts, or the spiritual and future blessings God gives.
senses.note: Spiritual 'good things to come' in HEB 9:11; HEB 10:1.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (46 uses) uses τὸ ἀγαθόν for the moral good believers are to do, and 'every good work' as the fruit God works in them.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter stresses doing good under hostility and keeping a 'good conscience'.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews speaks of the 'good things to come' that the law only foreshadowed.

study.translationNote: English 'good' renders both ἀγαθός and καλός. ἀγαθός tends to stress inner worth and benefit, καλός visible excellence or nobility, but the two overlap (both in LUK 8:15, 'a noble and good heart'). Versions vary in ROM 5:7 ('good man' or 'good person') and in rendering τὰ ἀγαθά as 'good things', 'goods' or 'blessings'.

background.note: In Homer ἀγαθός describes the noble, well-born or brave man, opposite to κακός 'base, cowardly'.
A votive inscription calls the emperor Nero 'good god' (ἀγαθὸς θεός), against which Jesus' 'no one is good but God' stands out.
Letters wish someone to arrive ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ, 'happily, with good fortune'.
A fortune-telling text promises 'master of many good things and possessions', as in LUK 12:19.

study.exegesisTip: Watch for the noun forms (τὸ ἀγαθόν 'the good', τὰ ἀγαθά 'good things') and the opposite word (πονηρός, κακός, φαῦλος), which shows which kind of goodness is meant.
study.caution: Interpreters disagree whether ROM 5:7 marks a real difference between a 'righteous' and a 'good' person, and on what Jesus implies about himself in MAR 10:18 ('Why do you call me good?').

study.summary: Good in a way that can be seen: beautiful or fine, well suited to its purpose, worthy in a role, morally noble and honourable, and right or fitting to do.

senses.label: Fine, beautiful, excellent
senses.definition: Fine in appearance or excellent in quality: beautiful stones, fine pearls, good wine.
senses.note: The original Greek sense is 'beautiful'.

senses.label: Good of its kind, useful
senses.definition: Sound and fit for its purpose: fruit, seed, soil, fish or salt that does what it should.
senses.note: Opposite σαπρός 'rotten, worthless' (MAT 12:33; MAT 13:48).

senses.label: Worthy in a role
senses.definition: Admirable in a given role or task: a good shepherd, soldier, servant or steward; a good fight.

senses.label: Morally noble, honourable
senses.definition: Morally fine and attractive, especially of 'good works' that others can see.
senses.note: Also 'good conduct' (JAM 3:13) and 'good conscience' (HEB 13:18).

senses.label: Right, what is right to do
senses.definition: As a noun (τὸ καλόν), what is right and honourable, which one should do and hold fast.
senses.note: Opposite κακός (ROM 12:17; 2CO 13:7).

senses.label: It is good / better
senses.definition: In the impersonal καλόν ἐστιν: 'it is good, fitting, or better' to do something.
senses.note: Often with comparative force 'it is better' (MAR 9:43; MAR 14:21), following Semitic idiom.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: The Pastoral Letters use καλός far more than other books: the law is good, 'good works', the 'good fight', the 'good deposit', the 'good confession'.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses καλός in the images of good fruit, good seed and good soil that show genuine discipleship.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John calls Jesus the 'good shepherd' and speaks of his 'good works' shown from the Father.

authorNotes.author: Peter
authorNotes.note: 1 Peter urges 'good conduct' among unbelievers so that they see the good works and glorify God.

study.translationNote: Nearly all versions say 'good', which hides the overtone of visible beauty and nobility. Some versions and commentators prefer 'noble' or 'model' shepherd (JOH 10:11), 'honourable' or 'noble deeds' (1PE 2:12), and 'right' (ROM 12:17; 2CO 13:7); καλόν is 'better' in MAR 14:21.

background.note: An early Christian letter entrusts a body to 'good and faithful' gravediggers, the same pairing as Matt 25:21.
A royal inscription trusts an oath 'because they are good (honest) men'.
A complaint speaks of people 'not using a good conscience', as in Heb 13:18.
A business letter contrasts good-quality (καλόν) drugs with rotten (σαπρόν) ones, as in Matt 12:33.

study.exegesisTip: Where καλός is used, ask what is being displayed: goodness others can recognise (MAT 5:16; 1PE 2:12) or fitness for a purpose (good soil, good shepherd).
study.caution: Hort's distinction that ἀγαθός is good in its effects and καλός is good as seen is useful but cannot always be pressed; the two words often overlap.

study.summary: First: first in order, time or place; former as opposed to later; first to act; foremost in rank or importance; and the leading people of a community. Christ is 'the First and the Last'.

senses.label: First in a series
senses.definition: The first of a sequence of people, days or things.
senses.note: 'The first day' of Unleavened Bread (MAR 14:12) or of the week (MAR 16:9).

senses.label: Former, earlier
senses.definition: The earlier of two, as opposed to the later or second; first state, first love, first covenant.
senses.note: Koine often uses πρῶτος for 'former' (πρότερος), so ACT 1:1 'first book' need not imply a third.

senses.label: First to act
senses.definition: Used where English has an adverb: someone does something first, before others.
senses.note: JOH 1:15 'he was before me' (πρῶτός μου).

senses.label: Chief, most important
senses.definition: Foremost in rank or importance: the first commandment, the best robe, the chief of sinners.

senses.label: Leading people
senses.definition: Plural, the leading men or women of a city or people.
senses.note: Esp. Luke–Acts.

senses.label: First and last (reversal)
senses.definition: In Jesus' sayings, those of high status now will be last in the kingdom, and greatness means service.

senses.label: Title: the First and the Last
senses.definition: A divine title of Christ, from Isa 44:6, expressing his eternity and sovereignty.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews contrasts the 'first' covenant and tent with the second and better one that replaces it.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke often mentions 'the leading men' of cities and peoples, and calls Philippi a 'first' (leading) city.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John's Revelation calls Christ 'the First and the Last' and announces that the first heaven and earth will pass away.

study.translationNote: Most versions use 'first', but 1TI 1:15 is 'chief' (KJV), 'worst' (NIV) or 'foremost' (ESV); JOH 1:15 is 'before me'; LUK 2:2 is 'the first census' (most) or 'before' (some); ACT 16:12 is 'a leading city' or 'chief city' of the district.

background.note: A return made 'since the first (former) return' shows πρῶτος meaning 'former', as in Acts 1:1.
A magical text has 'I am before you' (σοῦ πρῶτός εἰμι), the same construction as John 1:15.
Used of military rank, 'of the first company'.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether πρῶτος ranks (chief), sequences (first of several) or contrasts with a later one (former); with a genitive of a person it may mean 'before'.
study.caution: LUK 2:2 ('the first census' or 'a census before Quirinius') and ACT 16:12 (text and sense of 'first city of the district') are both debated.

study.summary: Child: a son or daughter and, more widely, descendants; used as a warm address, for an apostle's converts, for God's children, and in the idiom 'children of' meaning those who share someone's character.

senses.label: Child, offspring, descendants
senses.definition: A son or daughter of a parent; in the plural also descendants or posterity.
senses.note: Either sex; a son in MAT 21:28.

senses.label: Affectionate address
senses.definition: Vocative 'child', 'son', a kindly address from an elder or teacher to a younger person or disciple.

senses.label: Spiritual child of a teacher
senses.definition: A convert or disciple viewed as the spiritual offspring of the one who brought them to faith.

senses.label: Children of God
senses.definition: Those who belong to God's family by new birth or adoption and share his life and inheritance.
senses.note: Esp. John and Paul.

senses.label: True descendants by likeness
senses.definition: Those regarded as someone's children because they share his faith or conduct, especially 'children of Abraham'.
senses.note: 'Children of the promise' vs 'children of the flesh' (ROM 9:8).

senses.label: Characterised by or belonging to
senses.definition: Semitic idiom 'children of X': people marked by a quality or belonging to a place, such as children of light, of wrath, or of Jerusalem.
senses.note: Also inhabitants of a city (LUK 19:44; GAL 4:25).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John calls believers τέκνα θεοῦ, born of God, and keeps υἱός for Jesus; the Letters contrast children of God and children of the devil and call church members 'children'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul links being God's children with the Spirit's witness, heirship and the coming freedom of creation, and calls his converts his beloved children.

study.translationNote: The KJV renders τέκνα θεοῦ 'sons of God' in JOH 1:12 and 1JO 3:1–2, while modern versions have 'children of God', which keeps John's distinction between believers (τέκνα) and Jesus the Son (υἱός). Idioms like 'children of wrath' (EPH 2:3) are sometimes paraphrased ('deserving of wrath').

background.note: From τίκτω 'give birth'; in Homer τέκνα is paired with wives in 'wives and little children'.
τέκνον is a kindly address even to grown men: 'run, child, finish it'.
A petition complains that creditors carried off a man's infant children.

study.exegesisTip: Look at the genitive after τέκνα (of God, of Abraham, of light, of wrath): it shows whose family or character a person shares.
study.caution: Some (following Westcott) hold that τέκνον stresses shared nature by birth while υἱός stresses status and privilege; others think Paul uses the two interchangeably (ROM 8:14–17), so the distinction should not be pressed.

study.summary: Blood: literal blood, natural descent, 'flesh and blood' as frail humanity, bloodshed and blood-guilt, the blood of sacrifices, and above all Christ's blood as his atoning, covenant-making death.

senses.label: Literal blood
senses.definition: The red fluid of a living body, as in a haemorrhage, a wound, or Jesus' sweat 'like drops of blood'.
senses.note: The apostolic decree forbids eating blood (ACT 15:20; ACT 15:29; ACT 21:25). As an end-time portent the moon turns 'to blood' (ACT 2:20; REV 6:12), and waters become blood (REV 16:3).

senses.label: Natural descent, kinship
senses.definition: Blood as the bearer of human generation and common origin.
senses.note: 'Not of bloods' (JOH 1:13, plural) denies that birth into God's family comes by human lineage. ACT 17:26 'of one blood' is the Byzantine reading; many modern texts read 'from one man'.

senses.label: 'Flesh and blood': mere humanity
senses.definition: With σάρξ, human nature in its frailty and limits, contrasted with God or with spiritual powers.
senses.note: Order varies: σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα or αἷμα καὶ σάρξ (EPH 6:12; HEB 2:14).

senses.label: Bloodshed, violent death; blood-guilt
senses.definition: Blood shed in killing, hence murder or violent death, and the guilt or responsibility for it.
senses.note: 'Shed blood' (ἐκχέω αἷμα) = kill; 'his blood be on us' (MAT 27:25), 'your blood be on your own heads' (ACT 18:6) and 'innocent of the blood of all' (ACT 20:26) are formulas of responsibility. 'Blood money', 'Field of Blood' (MAT 27:6; ACT 1:19).

senses.label: Sacrificial blood
senses.definition: The blood of animal victims offered in the cult, applied to cleanse and to make atonement.
senses.note: 'Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness' (HEB 9:22).

senses.label: Christ's blood: his atoning death
senses.definition: Jesus' blood shed on the cross, standing for his sacrificial death that inaugurates the new covenant, redeems, justifies, cleanses and reconciles.
senses.note: Also in the Lord's Supper: 'the cup… a participation in the blood of Christ' (1CO 10:16; 1CO 11:25).

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews (21 uses) builds its argument on blood: the high priest's annual entry with animal blood is contrasted with Christ entering once 'by his own blood', whose blood 'speaks better than Abel's'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has the eucharistic-sounding 'drink my blood' discourse, the blood and water from Jesus' side, the cleansing blood of 1 John, and in Revelation the martyrs' blood and the saints washed in the Lamb's blood.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Acts uses Old Testament blood-guilt language for responsibility for death and for the preacher's duty, and speaks of the church God acquired 'with his own blood'.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses 'blood' as shorthand for Christ's sacrificial death: by it believers are justified, redeemed, brought near and reconciled.

study.translationNote: Versions agree on 'blood', but some (NLT, GNT) paraphrase 'by his blood' as 'by his death' or 'sacrifice' to make the meaning plain, and render 'flesh and blood' as 'any human being' (Matt 16:17; Gal 1:16). At Acts 17:26 the KJV's 'of one blood' follows a text with αἷμα; most modern versions read 'from one man'.

background.note: From Homer on, αἷμα is blood, and in tragedy streams of shed blood; it also meant bloodshed or murder.
The figurative 'blood of the grape' (wine) appears in the Septuagint wisdom literature, echoing Hebrew usage.
A Jewish prayer for vengeance on a tombstone at Rheneia speaks of those who 'poured out her innocent blood unjustly', paralleling the biblical 'shed innocent blood'.
An adoption deed calls the adoptee a son 'as if begotten of your own blood', illustrating blood as descent (cf. John 1:13).

study.exegesisTip: When blood is 'shed', 'required' or 'on' someone, think of death and responsibility; when it is Christ's blood, read it as a compact way of saying 'his sacrificial death' and its effects.
study.caution: Scholars debate whether 'the blood' of a sacrifice signifies life released and offered (Westcott and others, from Lev 17:11) or simply violent death (Stibbs, Morris); whether 'drink my blood' in John 6 refers to the Eucharist is also disputed.

study.summary: Bread or a loaf — the staple food of the ancient world — hence food in general and a meal; also the consecrated bread, the bread of the Lord's Supper, and Jesus as the 'bread of life'.

senses.label: Bread, a loaf
senses.definition: Baked bread, either as substance or as individual (flat, round) loaves.
senses.note: Plural ἄρτοι usually means 'loaves', as in the feeding miracles.

senses.label: Food, sustenance; a meal
senses.definition: Bread standing for food in general, and 'to eat bread' (a Hebraism) for taking a meal.
senses.note: 'Eat bread' = have a meal (LUK 14:1); 'eat someone's bread' = be supported by them (2TH 3:8).

senses.label: Consecrated bread (showbread)
senses.definition: The loaves set out before God in the sanctuary, which only priests could eat.
senses.note: ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως, literally 'loaves of the setting-forth'.

senses.label: Bread of the Lord's Supper
senses.definition: The bread Jesus took, blessed and broke at the Last Supper, and the bread broken in the church's common meal.
senses.note: 'The breaking of bread' (ACT 2:42). Paul: 'one bread, one body' (1CO 10:17).

senses.label: Jesus, the bread of life
senses.definition: Metaphorically, Jesus himself as the true bread from heaven that gives eternal life, surpassing the manna.
senses.note: Builds on the manna 'bread from heaven' (JOH 6:31).

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John (24 uses, almost all in ch. 6) moves from the loaves of the feeding to the manna and then to Jesus' claim 'I am the bread of life'.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark presses the meaning of the loaves: the disciples 'did not understand about the loaves', and in the boat they have only 'one loaf' yet worry about bread.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke makes 'breaking bread' a recognition and community motif: the risen Jesus is known 'in the breaking of the bread', and the church continues it.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'bread', 'loaf/loaves' and 'food' depending on context. In the Lord's Prayer (Matt 6:11) most keep 'daily bread', though the sense is daily food. The Hebraism 'eat bread' is often rendered simply 'eat' or 'have a meal' (Luke 14:1; Mark 3:20).

background.note: From Homer on, ἄρτος is a cake or loaf of wheat bread, contrasted with barley porridge (μᾶζα).
Household accounts list 'pure' (white) bread for children, showing ἄρτος as the everyday word.
A letter mentions a basket with four pairs of loaves, matching the gospel picture of loaves as countable units.

study.exegesisTip: Decide whether ἄρτος means a literal loaf, food or a meal in general, or carries the theological weight of the manna, the Supper, or Jesus himself.
study.caution: Whether John 6:51–58 refers to the Eucharist is debated; and since ἄρτος can denote unleavened as well as leavened bread, the word itself does not settle whether the Last Supper was a Passover meal.

study.summary: To teach: to give instruction, publicly or privately, especially Jesus' teaching in synagogue and temple, the apostles' and the church's instruction in the faith, and teaching by God or the Spirit.

senses.label: Teach, give instruction
senses.definition: To instruct people, often absolutely ('he was teaching'), especially Jesus' public teaching in synagogues, the temple or outdoors.
senses.note: Often paired with κηρύσσω 'proclaim' (MAT 4:23; MAT 11:1).

senses.label: Teach a content or way
senses.definition: To teach someone something: a doctrine, commandments, 'the way of God', or how to act.
senses.note: Double accusative 'teach them many things' (MAR 4:2); with ὅτι for content (MAR 8:31).

senses.label: Teaching as a church ministry
senses.definition: The ongoing instruction of believers in the apostolic message, a recognised gift and responsibility in the church.
senses.note: In the Pastorals linked to authority and sound doctrine (1TI 2:12; 1TI 4:11; 1TI 6:2).

senses.label: Be taught, receive instruction
senses.definition: Passive: to have learned by instruction, especially the received apostolic tradition.
senses.note: Paul denies he was 'taught' the gospel by men (GAL 1:12).

senses.label: Taught by God or the Spirit
senses.definition: Instruction given directly by the Father, the Holy Spirit or the 'anointing'.

senses.label: Teach error
senses.definition: To teach false or merely human doctrine, or to instruct someone into wrongdoing.
senses.note: REV 2:14 has the unusual dative of person (ἐδίδασκεν τῷ Βαλάκ).

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark repeatedly says Jesus taught, often 'began to teach', while recording relatively little of the content; when content is given it centres on the coming passion.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke presents Jesus' 'doing and teaching' as continued by the apostles, who keep teaching in Jesus' name despite bans, and by Paul until the end of Acts.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John stresses that Jesus taught openly in synagogue and temple, teaching what the Father taught him; in 1 John the anointing teaches believers.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: In the Pastoral Letters teaching becomes a defined, authorised task tied to 'sound doctrine' and its faithful transmission.

study.translationNote: Translation is almost uniformly 'teach'. Versions differ on the imperfect ἐδίδασκεν: 'taught', 'was teaching', or inceptive 'began to teach' (MSB, NIV in Mark 1:21). The pairing with 'preach' (κηρύσσω) is kept distinct in most versions.

background.note: Common from Homer on for instructing a person or teaching a skill, as when Phoenix taught Achilles to be 'a speaker of words and doer of deeds'.
A mother congratulates her son on finishing his education: now he will 'teach the children' and have a livelihood for old age.
In everyday letters the verb can simply mean 'inform, tell', as when a doctor is asked to 'tell me' what the solvent is.

study.exegesisTip: Note the object: whether a person, a content ('the way of God', 'these things') or both, and who the teacher is (Jesus, apostles, church leaders, God, false teachers).
study.caution: The scope of 'I do not permit a woman to teach' (1TI 2:12) is strongly debated: whether διδάσκειν means all teaching, authoritative doctrinal teaching, or is paired with αὐθεντεῖν to describe one domineering activity. C. H. Dodd's sharp distinction between 'teaching' (didache) and 'preaching' (kerygma) is also widely questioned.

study.summary: To put, place or lay something somewhere; to lay down (one's life, garments); to kneel; and to appoint or make someone something. The middle can mean to set in one's mind or resolve.

senses.label: Put, place, set
senses.definition: To put an object or person in a place: a lamp on a stand, a veil over a face, money at the apostles' feet, a stone in Zion, prisoners in custody.
senses.note: Of putting in prison (ACT 4:3; ACT 12:4); of serving wine (JOH 2:10); of laying money by (1CO 16:2).

senses.label: Lay the dead or sick
senses.definition: To lay a body in a tomb, or the sick where Jesus would pass.
senses.note: 'See the place where they laid him' (MAR 16:6).

senses.label: Lay down, lay aside
senses.definition: To put something off or down, especially to give up one's life voluntarily for others.
senses.note: τὴν ψυχὴν τιθέναι 'lay down one's life' is a Johannine idiom; Jesus also 'lays aside' his garments (JOH 13:4).

senses.label: Kneel
senses.definition: With τὰ γόνατα 'the knees': to bend the knee in prayer or (mock) homage.

senses.label: Appoint, make, destine
senses.definition: To set someone in a role or condition: God appoints to ministry, makes heir or father, destines not for wrath, puts enemies under Christ's feet.
senses.note: Often middle (ἔθετο). 'I have made you father of many nations' (ROM 4:17); 'until I make your enemies a footstool' (MAT 22:44).

senses.label: Set in the mind, resolve
senses.definition: Middle: to lay something up in one's heart, take to heart, or form a plan or decision.
senses.note: Largely Lukan.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses τίθημι for the Good Shepherd's voluntary death: he lays down his life and takes it up again, and believers ought likewise to lay down their lives for one another.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke favours the middle for decisions and inward reflection ('laid it up in their hearts', 'Paul resolved in the Spirit') and the phrase 'placing the knees' for kneeling in prayer.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses the word for God's sovereign appointing: placing members and gifts in the church, appointing to salvation, entrusting the message of reconciliation, appointing Paul as herald.

study.translationNote: Because τίθημι is so general, English varies widely: 'put', 'lay', 'place', 'set', 'appoint', 'make', 'destine'. In 1 Thess 5:9 'appointed' (KJV, ESV) and 'destined' (NRSV) differ in tone; in John 10 'lay down' (most) is paraphrased 'sacrifice' (NLT). 'Kneel' renders an idiom ('place the knees') that some literal versions keep.

background.note: Everyday instructions: 'put them in a safe place', showing the basic sense 'place, set'.
'Even if you have to pawn your cloak' (literally 'put it down as a pledge') illustrates 'lay down'.
The middle is used of drawing up a bond or a will ('for which you drew me up a bond'), close to the sense 'make, appoint'.

study.exegesisTip: Watch the voice and complements: active with a place ('put on/under'), with ψυχήν ('lay down life'), with γόνατα ('kneel'), or middle with a double object or εἰς ('appoint someone to/as').
study.caution: 1PE 2:8 ('to which they were also appointed', εἰς ὃ καὶ ἐτέθησαν) is debated: whether God appointed unbelievers to disobedience itself or to the stumbling that follows from it.

study.summary: To walk or walk about; then, following Hebrew usage, to 'walk' in the sense of living or conducting one's life according to some norm, power or sphere — Paul's and John's favourite verb for Christian behaviour.

senses.label: Walk, walk about
senses.definition: Literal walking or going about, including the lame walking when healed and Jesus walking on the sea.
senses.note: 'Get up and walk' and 'the lame walk' mark healing (MAT 9:5; MAT 11:5; ACT 3:8).

senses.label: Go about among, accompany
senses.definition: To move about in a place or among people, or to go about with someone as a follower.
senses.note: 'No longer walked with him' (JOH 6:66) = ceased to follow him as disciples.

senses.label: Live, conduct oneself
senses.definition: To live one's life in a certain manner, especially in ethical exhortation.
senses.note: With adverbs ('worthily', 'properly', 'disorderly': 2TH 3:11) and ἐν + sphere ('in newness of life').

senses.label: Live by a rule or standard
senses.definition: To live in accordance with a norm, custom or power: the customs, the flesh or the Spirit, love, 'as a mere human'.
senses.note: κατά + accusative or the dative of rule (πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε, GAL 5:16).

senses.label: Walk in light, darkness or truth
senses.definition: To live within a sphere — light or darkness, truth, the commandments — that shapes and reveals one's whole life.
senses.note: Characteristic of the Johannine writings.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (32 uses) makes 'walk' his main word for Christian conduct: in newness of life, by the Spirit, by faith not sight, in love, worthily of the calling, wisely toward outsiders.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: In the Gospel walking is often literal, but John turns it into the image of living in light or darkness; the letters speak of walking in the light, in truth and 'as he walked'.

study.translationNote: Formal versions (KJV, ESV, NASB) keep the Hebraic image 'walk'; functional ones (NIV, NLT, MSB in places) render the ethical uses 'live', 'behave' or 'conduct yourselves' (e.g. Col 4:5; 1 Thess 4:1, 12). 'Walk' preserves the picture of a continuous path; 'live' makes the moral sense plain.

background.note: In Attic Greek 'walk about', 'stroll'; also of philosophers who taught while walking (whence 'Peripatetic').
A prodigal son writes that he is 'going about in a disgraceful state', a literal-to-figurative use of the verb.
An epitaph says the miser 'is dead while he walks about and lives the life of a corpse', a parallel to Rev 3:1.

study.exegesisTip: In the letters, read περιπατέω as 'live, conduct your life' and look at the qualifier (adverb, κατά phrase, dative, ἐν phrase) that tells by what standard or in what sphere.

study.summary: The aorist (ἔφαγον) and future (φάγομαι) of 'eat', ἐσθίω: to eat or take food, have a meal, eat in questions of food law and conscience, partake spiritually, and figuratively devour.

senses.label: Eat, take food
senses.definition: To eat in the ordinary sense, or to go without food ('ate nothing').
senses.note: δοῦναι φαγεῖν 'give something to eat' (MAR 5:43; MAT 14:16; MAT 25:35).

senses.label: Eat a meal, eat the Passover
senses.definition: To share a meal or a festal meal, including the Passover and the consecrated bread.
senses.note: 'Eat bread' (Hebraism) = have a meal (MAR 3:20).

senses.label: Eat with regard to purity or conscience
senses.definition: Eating as a matter of ritual purity, food laws or idol meat, and of conscience toward others.

senses.label: Right to eat; be supported
senses.definition: Eating as a right or entitlement, especially being maintained at others' expense.

senses.label: Spiritual eating
senses.definition: Figuratively, receiving life by partaking of Jesus as bread from heaven, or eating from the tree of life.
senses.note: 'I have food to eat that you do not know about' (JOH 4:32).

senses.label: Devour, consume
senses.definition: Figuratively, to destroy as if eating: rust consuming flesh, the beast devouring the harlot, birds feeding on the slain.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John moves from physical eating at the feeding to the demand to 'eat the flesh of the Son of Man', and from food the disciples brought to Jesus' food of doing the Father's will.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul discusses eating chiefly as a matter of freedom, conscience and love in the community, and of not being a burden.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke features meals: the father's feast for the prodigal, the Last Supper Jesus longed to eat, the risen Jesus eating, and Peter's vision of unclean food.

study.translationNote: English simply has 'eat'. The infinitive φαγεῖν after 'give' or 'have' is often rendered as a noun: 'something to eat', 'food' (Mark 5:43; John 4:33; 1 Cor 9:4).
study.exegesisTip: Strong's lists φάγω (aorist/future) separately from ἐσθίω (present), so for a full word study of 'eat' look up both numbers; the tense difference is morphological, not a different meaning.
study.caution: Whether John 6:50–58 ('eat my flesh') refers primarily to faith in Jesus' death or to the Eucharist is debated.

study.summary: Of a father, to beget or become the father of; of a mother, to bear; passive, to be born. Figuratively, to bring into being: converts, quarrels, and believers 'born of God'.

senses.label: Beget, father
senses.definition: Of a man: to become the father of a child.
senses.note: The Matthean genealogy repeats ἐγέννησεν; at MAT 1:16 it switches to the passive of Jesus' birth from Mary.

senses.label: Bear, give birth
senses.definition: Of a woman: to bring forth a child.

senses.label: Be born; be conceived
senses.definition: Passive: to come into life by birth (or, in context, be conceived), including place or circumstances of birth.
senses.note: Of status by birth: 'I was born a citizen' (ACT 22:28).

senses.label: Born of God, born from above
senses.definition: Of believers brought into God's family by a new, divine origin.
senses.note: Characteristic of John (see author note).

senses.label: 'Today I have begotten you'
senses.definition: Quoting Psalm 2:7, God's declaration of the Messiah's sonship, applied to Jesus' resurrection and exaltation.

senses.label: Bring into being, produce
senses.definition: Figuratively, to cause or give rise to: Paul 'fathering' converts through the gospel, or foolish debates that 'breed' quarrels.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew (45 uses, mostly the genealogy) uses the formula 'A begot B', then breaks the pattern at Jesus: Mary, 'of whom Jesus was born', and the child 'conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit'.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John uses the verb for a new birth: 'born of God', 'born from above', 'of water and Spirit'; 1 John makes being born of God visible in righteousness, love and faith.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul contrasts birth 'according to the flesh' and 'according to the Spirit' (Hagar and Sarah) and calls himself the father of his converts.

authorNotes.author: Hebrews
authorNotes.note: Hebrews twice cites Psalm 2:7 for the Son's superiority and appointment as high priest, and recalls the descendants 'born' of Abraham.

study.translationNote: In Matthew 1 older versions say 'begat', modern ones 'was the father of' (NIV, ESV, MSB) or 'fathered'. In Ps 2:7 citations, 'today I have begotten you' (KJV, ESV) becomes 'today I have become your Father' (NIV, MSB). John 3:3 is 'born again' or 'born from above', because ἄνωθεν, not γεννάω, is ambiguous.

background.note: Mostly of the father ('the father who begot'), but also of the mother; in the middle, 'produce, create'.
Psalm 2:7, 'today I have begotten you', is the royal-sonship text the NT applies to Jesus.
Birth registrations use the formula 'we register the son born to us'.
An inscription honouring Augustus says a man might rightly think it would have been better not to live 'had he not been born' — compare Mark 14:21.

study.exegesisTip: Check who is the subject (father, mother, God) and whether the verb is active or passive; with ἐκ ('born of/from') the stress is on origin and therefore on character.
study.caution: In 1JO 5:18 'the one born of God keeps him' may refer to Christ (aorist participle) or to the believer, depending on the reading and interpretation. The 'today' of Psalm 2:7 is variously applied to the resurrection, the incarnation or eternal generation.

study.summary: A house or dwelling; by extension the household living in it and the property belonging to it; figuratively the body as the soul's tent and the Father's heavenly house.

senses.label: House, building
senses.definition: A dwelling place as a physical structure, built on rock or sand, entered or left.

senses.label: Home, place of hospitality
senses.definition: Someone's home as the setting of daily life, teaching, healing and hospitality.
senses.note: ἐν (τῇ) οἰκίᾳ 'at home, indoors'; 'receive into your house' (2JO 1:10).

senses.label: Household, family
senses.definition: The people living together in a house: family, servants and dependants.
senses.note: 'Caesar's household' (PHP 4:22) = members of the imperial staff, slaves and freedmen.

senses.label: Property, estate
senses.definition: A house as possession, hence one's property and means.
senses.note: 'Devour widows' houses' = seize their property.

senses.label: Body; heavenly dwelling
senses.definition: Figuratively, the earthly body as a tent-house, the eternal 'house' from God, and the Father's house with many rooms.
senses.note: 'In a great house' (2TI 2:20) pictures the church.

authorNotes.author: Mark
authorNotes.note: Mark often withdraws Jesus 'into the house' for private explanation to the disciples, away from the crowds.

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: Luke makes houses the base of mission and church life: the disciples stay in one house, Saul is found in Judas' house, the church prays in Mary's house, Peter lodges with Simon the tanner.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses οἰκία for the body as an earthly 'tent-house', for households as units of the church, and warns of false teachers who worm their way into houses.

study.translationNote: Versions vary between 'house', 'home' and 'household' depending on whether the building, the domestic setting or the people are meant (John 4:53 'household'; Phil 4:22 'Caesar's household'). In John 14:2 the 'mansions' of the KJV render the separate word μοναί; modern versions have 'rooms' in the Father's house.

background.note: In Herodotus and Attic prose the ordinary word for a building, house; κατ' οἰκίαν 'at home'.
Following Hebrew bayit, the Greek can stand for one's possessions, the background of 'widows' houses'.
A complaint distinguishes the whole house (οἰκία) from the mother's apartment (οἶκος) within it.
A deed concerns 'half of a three-storied house' inherited from a mother.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether the building, the home as setting, the people in it, or the property is in view; household language often carries early church life, since believers met and were baptised by households.
study.caution: The classical distinction between οἰκία (the dwelling) and οἶκος (the whole estate or household) is not consistently kept in the NT, so arguments built on the choice of word are weak. Whether 'household' conversions (e.g. JOH 4:53; 1CO 16:15) included infants is debated in discussions of baptism.

study.summary: A place: a spot or location, region, the place where something is or belongs, the temple as 'the holy place', a seat or room, and figuratively room or opportunity.

senses.label: Place, location
senses.definition: A spot or area in space, often described: desolate, level, waterless, rocky, or named (Golgotha).
senses.note: ἔρημος τόπος 'a lonely place' is frequent in the Gospels.

senses.label: Specific spot, proper position
senses.definition: The particular place where something lies, happened or belongs; also a passage in a book.
senses.note: 'Put your sword back into its place' (MAT 26:52); 'found the place where it was written' (LUK 4:17).

senses.label: Region, locality
senses.definition: A district or inhabited area and its people.
senses.note: κατὰ τόπους 'in various places' (MAT 24:7; MAR 13:8).

senses.label: Holy place, the temple
senses.definition: The sanctuary or temple as 'the (holy) place' where God is worshipped.
senses.note: Reflects Hebrew māqôm for the sanctuary.

senses.label: Seat, room, appointed place
senses.definition: Space or a position assigned to someone: a seat at table, room to stay, a prepared place, one's rightful lot.
senses.note: Also of a role: 'one who fills the place of the outsider' (1CO 14:16).

senses.label: Opportunity, room to act
senses.definition: Figuratively, scope, occasion or opportunity for something.
senses.note: 'Do not give the devil a foothold' (EPH 4:27).

authorNotes.author: Luke–Acts
authorNotes.note: In Acts 'this place' is the temple: Stephen is charged with speaking against it and Paul with defiling it; heaven is God's throne, so 'what is the place of my rest?'

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John contrasts the disputed 'place' of worship and the leaders' fear of losing their 'place' with the place Jesus goes to prepare for his own.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul uses τόπος metaphorically for room or opportunity: leave room for wrath, give no foothold to the devil, no more room for work in these regions.

study.translationNote: Usually 'place', but versions vary in figurative uses: Luke 2:7 'no room in the inn' or 'no place in the guest room'; Rom 12:19 'give place to wrath' (KJV) or 'leave room for God's wrath' (NIV, ESV); Eph 4:27 'give place' or 'foothold'; Heb 12:17 'no place for repentance' or 'no chance to change'.

background.note: In tragedy and later prose, a place or region; periphrastically 'the whole place of earth'.
The Septuagint renders māqôm by τόπος, including the 'holy place' of the sanctuary.
Inscriptions use τόπος for a reserved seat in a theatre, illustrating the seat at a banquet in Luke 14:10.
Clement of Rome, like Luke 4:17, uses τόπος of a passage in a book.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whether τόπος is a literal spot, a region, the temple, an assigned position, or an opportunity; with δίδωμι ('give place') it is usually figurative.
study.caution: In ROM 12:19 'give place to wrath' may mean leave room for God's judgement (most) or yield to your opponent's anger; in HEB 12:17 it is debated whether Esau found no room for his own repentance or for a change of mind in Isaac.

study.summary: Righteousness or justice: upright conduct that conforms to God's will, fairness in judging, God's own saving righteousness, and — especially in Paul — the right standing with God given through faith.

senses.label: Upright conduct
senses.definition: Doing what is right before God; ethical righteousness expressed in action.
senses.note: 'Do righteousness' (1JO 2:29; 1JO 3:7); 'pursue righteousness' (1TI 6:11).

senses.label: Justice, fairness
senses.definition: Just dealing, especially in judging or governing.
senses.note: God 'will judge the world in righteousness' (ACT 17:31).

senses.label: God's own righteousness
senses.definition: God's character as just and faithful, shown in his dealings with sin and in keeping his promises to save.
senses.note: In ROM 1:17 and ROM 3:21 'the righteousness of God' may also include the righteousness he gives (see caution).

senses.label: Right standing given by faith
senses.definition: The status of being right with God, credited or given to the believer through faith in Christ apart from works.
senses.note: λογίζεσθαι εἰς δικαιοσύνην 'credit as righteousness' (ROM 4:3, from Gen 15:6); 'the gift of righteousness' (ROM 5:17).

senses.label: Righteousness based on the law
senses.definition: The righteousness sought by keeping the law, which Paul contrasts with the righteousness of faith.
senses.note: 'Their own righteousness' versus God's (ROM 10:3; PHP 3:9).

senses.label: Righteousness as a ruling power
senses.definition: Righteousness personified as a master to whom believers, freed from sin, are now enslaved.
senses.note: Esp. Romans 6.

authorNotes.author: Paul
authorNotes.note: Paul (about 60 uses) concentrates on 'the righteousness of God' revealed in the gospel, righteousness 'by faith' versus 'from the law', and the believer becoming 'the righteousness of God' in Christ.

authorNotes.author: Matthew
authorNotes.note: Matthew uses δικαιοσύνη for the faithful doing of God's will that the kingdom requires and brings: Jesus fulfils 'all righteousness', disciples hunger for it, are persecuted for it, and must exceed the Pharisees in it.

authorNotes.author: James
authorNotes.note: James reads Abraham's faith 'credited as righteousness' together with his works, and says human anger does not produce God's righteousness.

authorNotes.author: John
authorNotes.note: John has the Spirit convict the world 'concerning righteousness' because Jesus goes to the Father; 1 John makes 'doing righteousness' the mark of God's children.

study.translationNote: English has two word-families (righteous/righteousness and just/justice/justify) for one Greek family, so versions must choose. Most use 'righteousness', but 'justice' appears where fairness is meant (e.g. Acts 17:31 in some versions). In Rom 1:17 the NIV 1984 had 'a righteousness from God' (the gift), the NIV 2011 and ESV 'the righteousness of God', and the NLT 'how God makes us right in his sight'. Older Catholic and Romance-language versions use 'justice' throughout.

background.note: In Greek thought δικαιοσύνη was justice as a civic and personal virtue, one of the cardinal virtues in Plato's Republic.
Genesis 15:6, Abraham's faith 'reckoned to him as righteousness', is the text Paul and James both expound.
The Septuagint occasionally uses δικαιοσύνη for Hebrew ḥesed ('steadfast love'), showing its covenantal, relational colouring.
The word is rare in papyri but common in inscriptions, where men are honoured for their 'righteousness and munificence'; similar virtue lists recall 2 Pet 1:5–7.

study.exegesisTip: Ask whose righteousness it is and in what sense: a quality of conduct, God's own character or saving action, a status given to believers, or justice in judgement; the genitive (θεοῦ) and prepositions (ἐκ πίστεως, ἐκ νόμου, εἰς) usually decide.
study.caution: 'The righteousness of God' in Paul (ROM 1:17; ROM 3:21) is intensely debated: God's own attribute, a righteous status from God, his saving and covenant-faithful action, or a combination. Whether Matthew's 'hunger for righteousness' (MAT 5:6) means ethical uprightness or God's vindicating justice is also disputed.
